questions.question: What does MCP stand for?

options.text: Model Context Protocol
Machine Communication Protocol
Model Control Process
Multi-Channel Platform

questions.explanation: MCP stands for Model Context Protocol, an open-source standard for connecting AI applications to external systems such as data sources, tools, and workflows.

questions.question: The official documentation compares MCP to which everyday technology?

options.text: A Wi-Fi router for AI models
A USB-C port for AI applications
A power adapter for LLMs
An HDMI cable for data sources

questions.explanation: The docs describe MCP as being like a USB-C port for AI applications: just as USB-C standardizes how devices connect, MCP standardizes how AI applications connect to external systems.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the categories of external systems MCP is designed to connect AI applications to?

options.text: Data sources (e.g., local files, databases)
Tools (e.g., search engines, calculators)
Workflows (e.g., specialized prompts)
GPU compute clusters for model training

questions.explanation: MCP connects AI applications to data sources, tools, and workflows. It does not concern itself with model training infrastructure.

questions.question: Which of the following projects is NOT part of the Model Context Protocol's official scope?

options.text: The MCP Specification
Language-specific MCP SDKs
A hosted LLM inference API
MCP reference server implementations

questions.explanation: MCP's scope includes the specification, SDKs, development tools (like the Inspector), and reference server implementations. MCP focuses solely on context exchange and does not dictate how AI applications use LLMs, nor does it provide model inference.

questions.question: According to the intro docs, what is the main benefit MCP delivers to developers?

options.text: Free hosting for AI applications
Reduced development time and complexity when building or integrating with AI applications and agents
Guaranteed model accuracy improvements
Automatic security auditing of servers

questions.explanation: For developers, MCP reduces development time and complexity: you build an integration once against a standard protocol instead of writing custom glue for every AI application.

questions.question: Which of the following applications is listed in the docs as supporting MCP?

options.text: Claude, ChatGPT, Visual Studio Code, and Cursor
Only Anthropic products
Only open-source terminal tools
MCP has no client support yet

questions.explanation: MCP is an open protocol with broad ecosystem support: AI assistants like Claude and ChatGPT, and development tools like Visual Studio Code, Cursor, and MCPJam all support it — making it possible to build once and integrate everywhere.

questions.question: Which of these is an example the docs give of what MCP can enable?

options.text: Claude Code generating an entire web app from a Figma design
Training a new foundation model from scratch
Replacing the operating system kernel
Compressing model weights for mobile devices

questions.explanation: Examples in the intro include agents accessing Google Calendar and Notion, Claude Code generating a web app from a Figma design, enterprise chatbots connecting to multiple databases, and AI models creating 3D designs in Blender.

questions.question: What benefit does MCP deliver to end users, according to the intro?

options.text: Cheaper API pricing
More capable AI applications that can access their data and take actions on their behalf when necessary
Faster model inference
Guaranteed privacy from all servers

questions.explanation: For end users, MCP results in more capable AI applications and agents which can access their data and take actions on their behalf when necessary.

questions.question: Besides servers and clients, what third kind of thing does the getting-started guide invite you to build?

options.text: MCP Apps — interactive apps that run inside AI clients
MCP Kernels
MCP Databases
MCP Browsers

questions.explanation: The Start Building section lists three paths: build servers (expose data and tools), build clients (applications that connect to servers), and build MCP Apps (interactive apps that run inside AI clients).

questions.question: Which languages have official MCP SDKs referenced across the documentation?

options.text: Python, TypeScript, Java, Kotlin, C#, Ruby, Rust, and Go
Python and JavaScript only
C and C++ only
PHP, Perl, and Bash

questions.explanation: The build-server quickstart provides parallel tutorials in Python, TypeScript, Java (Spring AI), Kotlin, C#, Ruby, Rust (rmcp), and Go — all backed by official SDKs under the modelcontextprotocol GitHub organization.

questions.question: Which of the following does MCP deliberately NOT specify?

options.text: How tools are discovered by clients
How AI applications use LLMs or manage the provided context
The message format between clients and servers
How servers describe their capabilities

questions.explanation: MCP focuses solely on the protocol for context exchange — it does not dictate how AI applications use LLMs or manage the context they receive. Discovery, message format, and capability description are all in scope.

questions.question: Which repositories live under the modelcontextprotocol GitHub organization?

options.text: Only the specification
The specification (with the schema), language SDKs, the MCP Inspector, and reference server implementations (servers)
Forks of popular LLM frameworks
Only closed-source binaries

questions.explanation: github.com/modelcontextprotocol hosts the specification (whose TypeScript schema is authoritative), the SDKs (python-sdk, typescript-sdk, kotlin-sdk, csharp-sdk, go-sdk, etc.), the inspector developer tool, and the servers repository of reference implementations like the filesystem server.

questions.question: SCENARIO: Your company builds an AI assistant that must integrate with 12 internal systems (databases, ticketing, wikis). Each new AI application you adopt currently requires re-writing all 12 integrations. How does adopting MCP change this?

options.text: It doesn't; every AI application still needs custom integrations
You build each integration once as an MCP server; any MCP-capable host (Claude, VS Code, ChatGPT, etc.) can then connect to all of them through the standard protocol
MCP merges all 12 systems into a single database
MCP only works with cloud systems, so internal systems are excluded

questions.explanation: This is MCP's core value proposition — like USB-C, it standardizes the connection. Build each integration once as an MCP server, and the growing ecosystem of MCP hosts can use them without additional glue code, reducing development time and complexity.

questions.question: SCENARIO: An enterprise wants employees to analyze data across several internal databases through a chat interface. Which MCP-enabled pattern from the intro docs matches this need?

options.text: An enterprise chatbot connecting to multiple databases across the organization via MCP servers, empowering users to analyze data using chat
Exporting all databases to CSV weekly
Fine-tuning a model on the databases
Giving every employee direct SQL access

questions.explanation: This is one of the intro's flagship examples: enterprise chatbots can connect to multiple databases across an organization through MCP, letting users analyze data conversationally.

questions.question: For whom does MCP 'reduce development time and complexity', and why is the protocol described as 'build once, integrate everywhere'?

options.text: For model trainers, because MCP compresses training data
For developers, because a server or client written against the open standard works across the whole ecosystem of MCP-supporting applications
For GPU vendors, because MCP reduces memory usage
For end users, because MCP removes the need for consent dialogs

questions.explanation: Because MCP is an open protocol supported across many clients and servers, developers build an integration once and it works everywhere MCP is supported — that's the 'build once and integrate everywhere' promise.

questions.question: What is the 'M×N integration problem' that MCP solves?

options.text: M models cannot share N GPUs

Without a standard, M AI applications each need custom integrations with N external systems (M×N connectors); MCP reduces this to M+N — each app implements the protocol once, each system exposes one MCP server
M users competing for N licenses
Matrix multiplication overhead in transformers

questions.explanation: This is the core economic argument for MCP: instead of every AI application writing bespoke connectors for every tool and data source (M×N pairings), each side implements the open standard once, collapsing the integration work to M+N.

questions.question: MCP explicitly takes inspiration from which earlier protocol, and what is the parallel?

options.text: HTTP/2 — both use binary framing

The Language Server Protocol (LSP) — just as LSP standardized adding programming-language support across an ecosystem of development tools, MCP standardizes integrating context and tools into the ecosystem of AI applications
SMTP — both route messages between servers
OAuth — both delegate authorization

questions.explanation: The specification states this directly: LSP solved the same shape of problem for editors and languages that MCP solves for AI applications and external systems — one protocol replacing per-pair integrations.

questions.question: According to the specification overview, MCP provides a standardized way for applications to do which three things?

options.text: Share contextual information with language models, expose tools and capabilities to AI systems, and build composable integrations and workflows
Train models, deploy models, and monitor models
Encrypt data, compress data, and cache data
Render UIs, store files, and send emails

questions.explanation: The spec's Overview names exactly these three: sharing contextual information with LLMs, exposing tools and capabilities to AI systems, and building composable integrations and workflows.

questions.question: Which top-level areas make up the MCP project and its documentation site?

options.text: Only the specification
Documentation, the Specification, Extensions, the Registry, SEPs (Specification Enhancement Proposals), and Community/governance
A model zoo and a benchmark suite
Frontend, backend, and database sections

questions.explanation: The project spans the docs/guides, the versioned specification, the optional Extensions framework, the MCP Registry for server discovery, the SEP process for proposing changes, and community governance (working groups, contributor ladder, policies).

questions.question: What is a Specification Enhancement Proposal (SEP)?

options.text: A paid support ticket

The formal mechanism for proposing changes to the MCP specification — markdown documents with PR-derived numbering, sponsors, and status labels (e.g., SEP-2575 made MCP stateless, SEP-1865 defined MCP Apps)
A server performance benchmark
A security exploit report

questions.explanation: SEPs drive protocol evolution: 2026-07-28 formalized a PR-based SEP workflow (SEP-1850) with markdown files in the seps/ directory, sponsor responsibilities, and status via PR labels. Major changes like statelessness (SEP-2575), MRTR (SEP-2322), and deprecations (SEP-2577) all arrived as SEPs.

questions.question: SCENARIO: A team of 5 AI products needs to integrate with 8 internal systems. Roughly how many integrations are needed without MCP versus with MCP?

options.text: 40 custom integrations without MCP; 13 protocol implementations (5 clients + 8 servers) with MCP
13 without; 40 with
8 either way
5 either way

questions.explanation: The M×N problem concretely: 5×8 = 40 bespoke connectors without a standard. With MCP, each product implements the client side once and each system exposes one server — 5+8 = 13 — and every future addition costs one implementation, not a row or column of connectors.

questions.question: In MCP's architecture, what is the role of the 'MCP Host'?

options.text: The program that provides context data to clients
The AI application that coordinates and manages one or multiple MCP clients
The transport layer that frames JSON-RPC messages
The authorization server that issues tokens

questions.explanation: The MCP host is the AI application (e.g., Claude Desktop, VS Code) that coordinates and manages MCP clients. Each client maintains a dedicated connection to one MCP server, and servers provide context to clients.

questions.question: How many MCP servers does a single MCP client connect to?

options.text: Exactly one — each client maintains a dedicated connection to one server
Up to ten servers per client
As many servers as the host configures
Two: one local and one remote

questions.explanation: The host creates one MCP client for each MCP server it connects to. Each client maintains a dedicated one-to-one connection with its corresponding server.

questions.question: Which two transport mechanisms does MCP support?

options.text: WebSocket and gRPC
Stdio and Streamable HTTP
TCP sockets and GraphQL
MQTT and Server-Sent Events only

questions.explanation: MCP supports the stdio transport (standard input/output for local processes) and the Streamable HTTP transport (HTTP POST with optional Server-Sent Events, used for remote servers).

questions.question: What underlying RPC protocol does MCP's data layer use?

options.text: gRPC
SOAP
JSON-RPC 2.0
REST over HTTP/2

questions.explanation: The data layer implements a JSON-RPC 2.0 based exchange protocol that defines message structure and semantics, and the same JSON-RPC format is used across all transports.

questions.question: As of protocol version 2026-07-28, MCP is described as a stateless protocol. What does this mean in practice?

options.text: Servers never store any data anywhere
Every request carries the protocol version and relevant capabilities in its _meta field, so servers can process each request on its own
Clients must reconnect after every request
Notifications are no longer supported

questions.explanation: Statelessness means each request is self-contained: the _meta field carries io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion and clientCapabilities (and normally clientInfo), so the server infers nothing from previous requests.

questions.question: Which request lets a client learn a server's supported protocol versions, capabilities, and identity in a single call?

options.text: initialize
server/discover
capabilities/get
server/handshake

questions.explanation: The mandatory server/discover request returns supportedVersions, the server's capabilities object, and serverInfo in _meta. Calling it is optional for clients, since every request already carries per-request metadata, but every server must implement it.

questions.question: How does a client opt in to receiving change notifications (such as tool list changes) from a server in protocol version 2026-07-28?

options.text: Notifications are always sent automatically to every connected client
The client polls notifications/poll every few seconds
The client opens a long-lived subscriptions/listen stream naming the notification types it wants
The client sets a webhook URL during initialization

questions.explanation: Change notifications are opt-in: the client sends a subscriptions/listen request with a notifications filter (e.g., toolsListChanged: true). The server acknowledges with notifications/subscriptions/acknowledged and delivers matching notifications on that stream.

questions.question: In a subscriptions/listen flow, what value does the io.modelcontextprotocol/subscriptionId field in each notification's _meta carry?

options.text: A random UUID generated per notification
The JSON-RPC ID of the subscriptions/listen request that opened the stream
The server's version string
A monotonically increasing sequence number

questions.explanation: Every notification on the stream carries a subscriptionId equal to the JSON-RPC ID of the subscriptions/listen request that opened it, letting clients correlate notifications with the subscription that produced them.

questions.question: What guarantee does MCP make about delivery of change notifications?

options.text: Exactly-once delivery is guaranteed
At-least-once delivery is guaranteed
Delivery is best effort; clients should also rely on polling to preserve freshness
Notifications are retried indefinitely until acknowledged

questions.explanation: Notifications are best effort — there is no guarantee every notification is sent or received, particularly across transport reconnects, so clients should also poll to keep results fresh.

questions.question: Which statement about local vs remote MCP servers is correct?

options.text: Local servers typically use the STDIO transport and serve a single client, while remote servers typically use Streamable HTTP and serve many clients
Local servers must use HTTP; remote servers must use STDIO
Remote servers cannot expose tools, only resources
A server's location changes its protocol semantics

questions.explanation: 'MCP server' refers to the program serving context regardless of where it runs. Local servers use STDIO and typically serve one client; remote servers use Streamable HTTP and typically serve many clients. The data layer semantics stay the same.

questions.question: In the 2026-07-28 spec, what are the ttlMs and cacheScope fields returned in results like server/discover and tools/list used for?

options.text: Rate limiting the client's requests
Caching: ttlMs is a freshness hint in milliseconds and cacheScope indicates who may reuse the response
Timing out slow tool calls
Configuring the transport keep-alive interval

questions.explanation: Results carry caching hints: ttlMs tells the client how long the result stays fresh (e.g., a tool list cacheable for five minutes), and cacheScope indicates who may reuse it (e.g., public). A cached list should also be treated as stale once a list_changed notification arrives.

questions.question: According to the specification overview, MCP takes inspiration from which existing protocol?

options.text: The Language Server Protocol (LSP)
The Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP)
The Border Gateway Protocol (BGP)
The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)

questions.explanation: The spec notes that MCP takes inspiration from the Language Server Protocol, which standardized language support across development tools; MCP similarly standardizes integrating context and tools into AI applications.

questions.question: What is the authoritative source of truth for the MCP specification's protocol requirements?

options.text: The TypeScript schema (schema.ts) in the specification repository
A PDF published annually
The Python SDK source code
The MCP Inspector's behavior

questions.explanation: The specification defines the authoritative protocol requirements based on the TypeScript schema in schema.ts for each protocol version (e.g., schema/2026-07-28/schema.ts).

questions.question: SCENARIO: A client sends a request declaring protocol version 2026-07-28 in _meta, but the server only supports 2025-11-25. What happens according to the discovery/versioning model?

options.text: The server silently downgrades and answers in the older format
The server rejects the request with an UnsupportedProtocolVersionError listing the versions it supports, and the client retries with a mutually supported version
The transport connection is terminated with no explanation
The server forwards the request to a newer server

questions.explanation: If a server doesn't support the requested version, it rejects the request with an UnsupportedProtocolVersionError (-32022) whose data lists supported versions; the client can then retry with a version both sides support. server/discover's supportedVersions lets clients learn this up front.

questions.question: How do the data layer and transport layer relate conceptually in MCP?

options.text: The data layer is the inner layer (JSON-RPC protocol, primitives) and the transport layer is the outer layer (connections, framing, authorization)
They are the same layer viewed from different sides
The transport layer defines tools; the data layer defines HTTP headers
The data layer only exists for stdio servers

questions.explanation: Conceptually the data layer (JSON-RPC 2.0 exchange, discovery, primitives, notifications) is the inner layer, wrapped by the transport layer (stdio or Streamable HTTP), which handles connection establishment, message framing, and authorization while keeping the same JSON-RPC format everywhere.

questions.question: SCENARIO: An MCP host connects to 3 different MCP servers, and one of those servers (a remote one) also serves 50 other users' hosts. Describe the cardinality correctly.

options.text: The host instantiates 3 MCP clients — one per server, each holding a dedicated 1:1 connection; the remote server meanwhile serves many clients (one per connected host)
One client multiplexes all 3 servers
Each server requires 3 clients
Hosts connect to servers directly without clients

questions.explanation: Cardinality: Host → many clients; each client ↔ exactly one server (dedicated connection). Local STDIO servers typically serve a single client, while remote Streamable HTTP servers typically serve many clients across hosts.

questions.question: How does Streamable HTTP differ from the legacy HTTP+SSE transport it replaced?

options.text: They are identical apart from the name

Legacy HTTP+SSE used separate endpoints (a long-lived GET/SSE channel plus a POST endpoint); Streamable HTTP (introduced 2025-03-26) uses a single MCP endpoint where POST carries client messages with optional SSE streaming on the response — and HTTP+SSE is now formally Deprecated
Streamable HTTP requires WebSockets
HTTP+SSE was faster and remains recommended

questions.explanation: Streamable HTTP replaced the two-endpoint HTTP+SSE design with a single endpoint supporting POST plus optional SSE streaming. The 2026-07-28 revision reclassified HTTP+SSE as Deprecated under the lifecycle policy, with migration to Streamable HTTP.

questions.question: How does capability negotiation differ between the legacy and modern protocol eras?

options.text: There is no capability negotiation in either era

Legacy (≤2025-11-25): capabilities are exchanged once in the initialize handshake and apply to the whole session. Modern (2026-07-28): negotiation is per-request — the client declares clientCapabilities in every request's _meta, and the server's capabilities are discoverable via server/discover
Capabilities are negotiated in DNS TXT records
Only servers declare capabilities; clients never do

questions.explanation: Capability negotiation ensures unsupported operations are never attempted. Legacy sessions negotiated once at initialize; the stateless modern era moved this to per-request metadata plus the mandatory server/discover RPC, and MissingRequiredClientCapabilityError (-32021) fires when a needed client capability wasn't declared.

questions.question: SCENARIO: In the docs' example, Visual Studio Code connects to the Sentry MCP server and then also to the local filesystem server. What happens inside VS Code?

options.text: One shared client object handles both servers
The VS Code runtime (the host) instantiates one MCP client object per connection — a second client is created for the filesystem server, each maintaining its own dedicated connection
Sentry proxies the filesystem traffic
VS Code must restart between servers

questions.explanation: This example illustrates the participant model: VS Code acts as the MCP host; connecting to each additional server instantiates an additional MCP client object dedicated to that server.

questions.question: In the 2026-07-28 revision, what replaced the initialize/notifications/initialized handshake?

options.text: A new handshake/start method that must be called once per connection
Every request carries its protocol version and client capabilities in _meta; server/discover is available for up-front discovery
An HTTP-only Mcp-Session-Id header that carries the negotiated capabilities
A TLS extension that embeds the protocol version in the certificate

questions.explanation: SEP-2575 removed the handshake entirely. Each request self-describes via _meta (io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion and clientCapabilities), and clients MAY call server/discover for up-front version/capability discovery. (Spec 2026-07-28 changelog, major change 2-3.)

questions.question: Which _meta fields are REQUIRED on every client request in protocol version 2026-07-28?

options.text: io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion, clientCapabilities, and clientInfo
io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion and clientCapabilities only
io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo and clientCapabilities only
io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion only

questions.explanation: protocolVersion and clientCapabilities are required on every request. clientInfo is a SHOULD (recommended but optional), and logLevel is optional. A common trap is treating clientInfo as required. (Spec basic/index, per-request protocol fields table.)

questions.question: A request arrives missing the required io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities _meta field. What must the server return?

options.text: -32021 MissingRequiredClientCapability
-32602 Invalid params, and on HTTP a 400 Bad Request status
-32600 Invalid request, and on HTTP a 401 status
It should process the request assuming empty capabilities

questions.explanation: A request missing a required _meta field is malformed: the server MUST reject it with -32602 (Invalid params) and HTTP 400. -32021 is different: it applies when the fields are present but a needed capability was not declared. (Spec basic/index.)

questions.question: A client's request includes valid _meta, but processing it requires a capability the client did not declare in clientCapabilities. What does the spec require?

options.text: The server proceeds and hopes the client can handle the response
The server returns -32602 Invalid params
The server returns MissingRequiredClientCapabilityError (-32021) with data.requiredCapabilities listing what is missing, HTTP 400
The server silently downgrades to a reduced feature set

questions.explanation: A server MUST NOT rely on capabilities the client has not declared. If a needed capability is absent, it MUST return -32021 with data.requiredCapabilities listing the missing capabilities (HTTP 400). (Spec basic/index.)

questions.question: Which statement about server/discover is correct in 2026-07-28?

options.text: Clients MUST call it before any other request
Servers MUST implement it; clients MAY call it (e.g., for up-front version selection or as a stdio backward-compatibility probe)
It is optional for servers but mandatory for clients on stdio
It replaces tools/list, prompts/list, and resources/list

questions.explanation: Servers MUST implement server/discover, but calling it is optional for clients - a client can invoke any RPC inline and handle UnsupportedProtocolVersionError. It is useful for presenting server info in one request and as the stdio legacy-vs-modern probe. (Spec server/discover.)

questions.question: Which set of information does a server/discover result carry?

options.text: supportedVersions, capabilities (including extensions), serverInfo in _meta, optional instructions, plus ttlMs and cacheScope
Only supportedVersions and a session token
The complete tools, prompts, and resources catalogs
The server's OAuth client_id and scopes_supported

questions.explanation: DiscoverResult includes supportedVersions, capabilities, _meta['io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo'], and optional instructions; the operation supports caching, so it also carries ttlMs and cacheScope. It does not return full primitive catalogs. (Spec server/discover.)

questions.question: A stdio server keeps a long-lived process per client and infers 'this connection already told me its capabilities' from an earlier request. Why does this violate 2026-07-28?

options.text: stdio servers must restart after each request
Servers MUST NOT rely on prior requests over the same connection for context; an open connection is not a session, and clients may interleave unrelated requests on one transport
Capabilities may only be transmitted over HTTP headers
It is allowed, as long as the process was launched by the client

questions.explanation: MCP is stateless: every request supplies its own metadata in _meta, and connection or process identity is explicitly not a proxy for session continuity. Cross-request state must use explicit identifiers passed on each request. (Spec basic/index, Statelessness.)

questions.question: A Streamable HTTP response stream breaks mid-request in the modern era. What must the client do?

options.text: Reconnect with the Last-Event-ID header to resume the stream
Send notifications/resume with the old request ID
Re-issue the lost request as a new request with a new request ID
Wait for the server to replay missed SSE events

questions.explanation: SSE resumability (Last-Event-ID and event IDs) was removed in 2026-07-28. A broken response stream loses the in-flight request; the client MUST re-issue it as a new request with a new ID. (Spec 2026-07-28 changelog, major change 9.)

questions.question: Which statement about the resultType field is FALSE under 2026-07-28?

options.text: A result with an unrecognized resultType value must be considered invalid by the client
Clients must treat an absent resultType from an earlier-protocol server as "complete"
Extensions may add resultType values, but only ones advertised via capabilities count as supported
A modern server may omit resultType on small results to save bytes

questions.explanation: Every result MUST include resultType in 2026-07-28 - there is no size exception. The other three statements are the exact spec rules: unrecognized values are invalid, absence from legacy servers means "complete", and extensions extend the value set via advertised capabilities. (Spec basic/index, ResultType.)

questions.question: Where does a modern server identify itself, and how much should clients trust that identity?

options.text: In io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo within each result's _meta (SHOULD); it is self-reported and must not drive security decisions
In a signed X-Server-Identity HTTP header that clients MUST verify
Only in the server/discover response; other results never carry identity
In the OAuth token's aud claim

questions.explanation: Servers SHOULD include io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo in every result's _meta. It is self-reported, intended for display/logging/debugging; implementations SHOULD NOT change behavior or make security decisions based on it. (Spec basic/index, per-response protocol fields.)

questions.question: What are the three core primitives that MCP servers can expose?

options.text: Tools, Resources, and Prompts
Functions, Files, and Formats
Actions, Events, and Streams
Tools, Agents, and Memories

questions.explanation: Servers expose Tools (executable functions), Resources (read-only data sources providing context), and Prompts (reusable interaction templates).

questions.question: Who 'controls' each server primitive according to the interaction model in the docs?

options.text: Tools: user, Resources: model, Prompts: application
Tools: model, Resources: application, Prompts: user
Tools: application, Resources: user, Prompts: model
All three are controlled by the model

questions.explanation: Tools are model-controlled (the LLM decides when to invoke them), resources are application-driven (the host decides how to retrieve and use them), and prompts are user-controlled (requiring explicit invocation, e.g., via slash commands).

questions.question: Which pair of protocol methods is used to discover and execute tools?

options.text: tools/find and tools/run
tools/list and tools/call
tools/get and tools/invoke
list/tools and call/tools

questions.explanation: Clients discover tools with tools/list (returning definitions with JSON Schemas) and execute a specific tool with tools/call.

questions.question: What schema language does MCP use to define and validate tool inputs?

options.text: Protocol Buffers
XML Schema (XSD)
JSON Schema
GraphQL SDL

questions.explanation: Each tool declares an inputSchema in JSON Schema, which enables type validation and documents required and optional parameters. Tools may also declare an optional outputSchema.

questions.question: How is a Resource uniquely identified in MCP?

options.text: By a sequential integer ID assigned by the client
By a unique URI, e.g., file:///path/to/document.md
By its SHA-256 content hash
By a (server name, index) tuple

questions.explanation: Each resource has a unique URI (such as file:///path/to/document.md) and declares its MIME type for appropriate content handling.

questions.question: What distinguishes a Resource Template from a Direct Resource?

options.text: Templates are write-enabled while direct resources are read-only
Templates use dynamic URIs with parameters (e.g., travel://activities/{city}/{category}) while direct resources have fixed URIs
Templates can only return JSON
Templates are discovered via tools/list

questions.explanation: Direct resources are fixed URIs pointing to specific data; resource templates are dynamic URIs with parameters that enable flexible queries, discovered via resources/templates/list, and they support parameter completion.

questions.question: Which protocol method retrieves the full definition of a specific prompt, including its arguments?

options.text: prompts/get
prompts/read
prompts/call
prompts/fetch

questions.explanation: prompts/list discovers available prompts, and prompts/get retrieves a full prompt definition with its arguments.

questions.question: A client wants to be notified when a specific resource changes. How does it accomplish this in the 2026-07-28 protocol?

options.text: By calling resources/subscribe with the URI
By sending a subscriptions/listen request with the resource URIs listed in the resourceSubscriptions filter
By re-reading the resource on a timer; there is no notification mechanism
By setting watch: true in resources/read

questions.explanation: To watch resources, the client sends subscriptions/listen with the URIs in the resourceSubscriptions filter; the server delivers notifications/resources/updated on the resulting stream whenever a watched resource changes.

questions.question: In the tools/call response, tool output is returned in which structure?

options.text: A single plain string field named output
A content array of typed content objects (e.g., type: "text")
A base64-encoded blob
An HTML document

questions.explanation: Tool responses return a content array of content objects, each with a type field (text, images, resources, etc.), enabling rich multi-format responses.

questions.question: Which UI patterns do applications typically use to expose user-controlled prompts?

options.text: Slash commands, command palettes, dedicated buttons, and context menus
Only automatic invocation by the model
Hidden system prompts the user never sees
Email digests

questions.explanation: Prompts require explicit invocation, and applications commonly expose them via slash commands (e.g., /plan-vacation), command palettes, dedicated UI buttons, and context menus.

questions.question: SCENARIO: You're building an MCP server for a database. You want to expose (a) a way to run queries, (b) the database schema for context, and (c) few-shot examples showing how to query well. Which primitives map to (a), (b), and (c)?

options.text: (a) Tool, (b) Resource, (c) Prompt
(a) Resource, (b) Prompt, (c) Tool
(a) Prompt, (b) Tool, (c) Resource
All three should be tools

questions.explanation: This is the exact example from the architecture docs: a database server exposes tools for querying, a resource containing the schema, and a prompt with few-shot examples for interacting with the tools.

questions.question: SCENARIO: A tool is registered as 'calculate' on a server that may later add currency conversion and unit conversion tools. Following the naming guidance from the tool discovery docs, what should you do?

options.text: Keep 'calculate'; shorter names save tokens
Use a clearer, namespaced-style name such as 'calculator_arithmetic' so the name uniquely and descriptively identifies the operation within the server's namespace
Use a random UUID as the name
Names don't matter because the title field is what the model sees

questions.explanation: The docs recommend names follow a clear naming pattern (e.g., calculator_arithmetic rather than just calculate). The name is the unique identifier and primary key for execution within the server's namespace, so descriptive, unambiguous names improve tool selection.

questions.question: SCENARIO: A user is filling in the {city} parameter of the resource template weather://forecast/{city}/{date} and types 'Par'. What MCP feature lets the application suggest 'Paris' or 'Park City'?

options.text: Sampling
Parameter completion on resource templates (also supported by prompts)
Tool annotations
Progress notifications

questions.explanation: Dynamic resources support parameter completion: typing 'Par' can suggest 'Paris' or 'Park City', helping users discover valid values without knowing exact formats. Prompts support argument completion similarly.

questions.question: Which method discovers Resource Templates specifically (as opposed to direct resources)?

options.text: resources/list
resources/templates/list
templates/get
resources/discover

questions.explanation: resources/list returns direct resource descriptors, while resources/templates/list returns resource template definitions (uriTemplate, name, title, description, mimeType). resources/read retrieves contents.

questions.question: What human-oversight mechanisms do the docs suggest applications implement around model-controlled tools?

options.text: None; tools should run silently
Approval dialogs for executions, permission settings for pre-approving safe operations, UI display of available tools, and activity logs of executions
A mandatory 24-hour delay before any tool runs
Only server-side logging

questions.explanation: Because tools are model-controlled, MCP emphasizes human oversight: showing available tools in the UI, approval dialogs for individual executions, permission settings for pre-approved safe operations, and activity logs showing executions with results.

questions.question: Which content block types can appear in a tool result's content array?

options.text: Only plain text
Text, images, audio, resource links, and embedded resources
Text and video only
Raw binary streams without type information

questions.explanation: Tool results are arrays of typed content blocks: text content, image content, audio content (both base64 with a mimeType), resource links (a URI reference without inline contents), and embedded resources (full resource contents inside the result).

questions.question: What's the difference between a resource link and an embedded resource in a tool result?

options.text: They are synonyms

A resource link references a resource by URI without carrying its contents (the client may fetch it via resources/read); an embedded resource carries the full resource contents inline within the result
Resource links are only for images
Embedded resources must be fetched separately

questions.explanation: Links defer the payload — useful for large or optional data the client can read on demand; embedded resources inline the payload so no follow-up read is needed.

questions.question: How are binary payloads like images and audio carried in MCP content blocks?

options.text: As raw bytes appended after the JSON
Base64-encoded in the block's data field, accompanied by a mimeType so the client knows how to interpret them
As URLs only — binary data cannot travel inline
As hexadecimal strings in the params

questions.explanation: JSON-RPC is text-based, so image/audio content blocks carry base64 data plus a mimeType (e.g., image/png, audio/wav). Large binaries can alternatively be exposed as resources and referenced by link.

questions.question: During a conversation, the LLM decides on its own that calling get_weather would help answer the user, and the host shows an approval prompt before executing. Which primitive and control model is this?

options.text: A Prompt - user-controlled
A Resource - application-controlled
A Tool - model-controlled, with human oversight via approval
A Root - host-controlled

questions.explanation: Tools are model-controlled: the LLM decides when to invoke them, while the host keeps a human in the loop (visibility, per-call approval, pre-approval settings, activity logs). (MCP docs, server concepts control model.)

questions.question: A host application automatically attaches the contents of file:///project/README.md to the model's context before a chat turn, without the model or the user asking. Which control model is exercised?

options.text: Model-controlled, because the content reaches the model
Application-controlled - Resources are retrieved and used at the host's discretion
User-controlled, because the user owns the file
Server-controlled, because the server exposes the URI

questions.explanation: Resources are application-driven: the host decides how and when to retrieve them and how to use them. Tools are model-controlled and Prompts are user-controlled - the classic Model->Tools, App->Resources, User->Prompts mapping. (MCP docs, server concepts.)

questions.question: A user types the /code-review slash command, which the client fetched from a server via prompts/list. Which control model does this demonstrate?

options.text: Model-controlled
Application-controlled
User-controlled
Transport-controlled

questions.explanation: Prompts are user-controlled templates: they require explicit user invocation, typically surfaced as slash commands or menu entries. (MCP docs, server concepts.)

questions.question: A tool's downstream API returns HTTP 500 while executing tools/call. What should the MCP server return?

options.text: A JSON-RPC error response with code -32603
A normal result (resultType "complete") whose payload sets isError: true and describes the failure
resultType "input_required" so the client can retry
HTTP 500 with an empty body

questions.explanation: Tool *execution* failures are reported inside the result via isError: true, so the model can see and react to the failure. JSON-RPC errors are reserved for protocol-level problems (unknown tool, invalid params, server bugs). (MCP docs, tools; a classic exam trap.)

questions.question: Two different servers connected to the same host both expose a tool named search. Who is responsible for disambiguating?

options.text: The spec forbids connecting both servers simultaneously
Tool names must be globally unique across the ecosystem, so one server is non-compliant
Tool names are unique per server; handling cross-server collisions (e.g., prefixing) is the host's responsibility
The registry rejects duplicate tool names at publish time

questions.explanation: Uniqueness is scoped to a single server. When multiple servers collide, the host disambiguates - commonly by prefixing tool names with a server identifier. (MCP docs, server concepts.)

questions.question: Which of the following is one of the spec's Security and Trust key principles, stated correctly?

options.text: Tool descriptions and annotations are considered untrusted unless obtained from a trusted server
Servers must sandbox every tool in a container
Hosts may transmit resource data to third parties as long as it is encrypted
User consent is only required for write operations, not reads

questions.explanation: Under Tool Safety, tools represent arbitrary code execution and descriptions/annotations are untrusted unless from a trusted server. The other statements contradict the principles: hosts must not transmit resource data elsewhere without consent, and explicit consent covers all data access and operations. (Spec 2026-07-28 overview, Security and Trust.)

questions.question: What does the Elicitation client feature allow an MCP server to do?

options.text: Request LLM completions from the client
Request specific information or input from the user during an interaction
Read arbitrary files on the client machine
Register new tools on the client

questions.explanation: Elicitation gives servers a structured way to request information from users on demand — for example, asking for seat preferences or booking confirmation — instead of requiring all information up front.

questions.question: Which two modes does elicitation support in the 2026-07-28 protocol?

options.text: Sync mode and async mode
Form mode and URL mode
Text mode and voice mode
Inline mode and modal mode

questions.explanation: Form mode has the client collect structured data from the user against a schema; URL mode has the user open a URL so the interaction happens out of band — suitable for sensitive flows like credential entry or third-party OAuth.

questions.question: How is an elicitation/create request delivered to the client in protocol version 2026-07-28?

options.text: As a server-initiated JSON-RPC request over a reverse channel

Via the Multi Round-Trip Requests (MRTR) pattern: the server responds to the original request with an InputRequiredResult whose inputRequests carry the elicitation, and the client retries the original request with inputResponses
By email to the registered user
As an HTTP 302 redirect

questions.explanation: Elicitation follows the MRTR pattern. When a server needs user input mid-request (e.g., during tools/call), it returns an InputRequiredResult containing elicitation/create requests; the client gathers input and retries the original request, attaching inputResponses and echoing any requestState.

questions.question: Why should servers use URL mode instead of form mode when requesting credentials such as passwords or API keys?

options.text: URL mode is faster to render
Form mode has a character limit
URL mode keeps the sensitive data out of band, so it never passes through the client or the LLM context
Form mode is deprecated

questions.explanation: Servers must not use form mode for sensitive information like passwords, API keys, tokens, or payment credentials. URL mode keeps the interaction between the user and the target site, so the data never passes through the client or the LLM context.

questions.question: Which client primitives are deprecated as of protocol version 2026-07-28?

options.text: Elicitation and notifications
Sampling and roots (and protocol-level logging on the server side)
Tools and prompts
Nothing has been deprecated

questions.explanation: Sampling and roots are deprecated as of 2026-07-28 and scheduled for removal. New implementations should integrate directly with LLM provider APIs (instead of sampling) and pass directories via tool parameters, resource URIs, or configuration (instead of roots). Protocol logging via notifications/message is also deprecated in favor of stderr/OpenTelemetry.

questions.question: Before its deprecation, what was the purpose of the Roots feature?

options.text: Granting servers superuser (root) access
Communicating filesystem boundaries — file:// URIs indicating directories where servers should focus their operations
Defining the root JSON-RPC endpoint
Pinning TLS root certificates

questions.explanation: Roots were file:// URIs that told servers which directories were in scope. Importantly, they were a coordination mechanism, not a security boundary — the spec said servers SHOULD respect them, and real enforcement belongs at the OS level.

questions.question: In a (now deprecated) sampling request, what do the modelPreferences priority fields express?

options.text: costPriority, speedPriority, and intelligencePriority — relative weights guiding the client's model selection
The exact model version the client must use, with no flexibility
GPU memory limits for inference
The order in which tools should be called

questions.explanation: modelPreferences included model hints plus costPriority, speedPriority, and intelligencePriority values (0–1) so the client could pick an appropriate model while keeping full control over permissions and security.

questions.question: What is the key distinction between an MCP 'host' and an MCP 'client'?

options.text: There is none; the terms are interchangeable
The host is the application users interact with, while clients are the protocol-level components that each handle one server connection
The host runs remotely and the client runs locally
The client manages the UI while the host manages the network

questions.explanation: The host application (like Claude.ai or an IDE) manages the overall user experience and coordinates multiple clients; each client handles direct communication with exactly one server.

questions.question: Which method does a server use to request user input via elicitation?

options.text: elicitation/create
user/ask
input/request
elicit/form

questions.explanation: Servers request user input with elicitation/create requests, delivered inside an InputRequiredResult via the Multi Round-Trip Requests pattern.

questions.question: How does a client tell a server that it supports elicitation?

options.text: By declaring "elicitation": {} in the io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities field of each request's _meta
By sending elicitation/enable once
By setting an HTTP header X-Elicitation: on
Support is assumed for all clients

questions.explanation: Client capabilities travel with every request in _meta under io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities; declaring elicitation there tells the server it can gather additional input from the user when requested.

questions.question: SCENARIO: While processing a tools/call to finalize a vacation booking, your server realizes it needs the traveler's seat preference and booking confirmation. What is the appropriate mechanism?

options.text: Fail the call with an error telling the user to retry with more arguments

Respond with an InputRequiredResult carrying a form-mode elicitation/create request with a schema (e.g., confirmBooking boolean, seatPreference enum), then complete the retried call using the user's responses
Silently pick a window seat
Email the user a form

questions.explanation: This is the elicitation pattern: rather than failing when data is missing, the server pauses via MRTR, requests structured input against a schema, and the client retries the original request with the collected inputResponses.

questions.question: When a client receives an elicitation request, which options must the user have?

options.text: Only 'submit'; declining is not part of the model
Provide the requested information, decline to provide it (optionally explaining why), or cancel the entire operation
Approve within 30 seconds or the server crashes
Forward the request to another user

questions.explanation: Elicitation is designed to respect user autonomy: users can provide the information through appropriate UI controls, decline with an optional explanation, or cancel the operation. Clients validate responses against the schema before returning them.

questions.question: SCENARIO: A server sends a URL-mode elicitation asking the user to authorize a third-party account. Which client behavior is correct per the docs?

options.text: The client fetches the URL itself to save the user a step

The client shows the full URL, gathers explicit consent before opening it, never fetches it automatically, and only learns whether the user consented — the interaction stays between the user and the target site
The client embeds the URL in an invisible iframe
The client extracts credentials from the page and returns them to the server

questions.explanation: For URL mode, clients show the full URL and require explicit consent before opening it, and never fetch it automatically. The client only learns whether the user consented; the data exchanged stays out of band, which is exactly why URL mode suits credential and OAuth flows.

questions.question: What should new implementations do instead of using the deprecated sampling primitive?

options.text: Use roots instead
Integrate directly with LLM provider APIs
Poll the client for completions
Embed a local model in every server

questions.explanation: Sampling is deprecated as of 2026-07-28 and scheduled for removal; the docs direct new implementations to integrate directly with LLM provider APIs.

questions.question: When (deprecated) sampling requests include tool use, what constraint applies?

options.text: The tools must be ones the server already exposes via tools/list

Clients declare support through the sampling.tools capability, and servers must not send tool-enabled sampling requests to clients that haven't declared it; the tool definitions are scoped to that sampling request
Tool use in sampling is unrestricted
Only read-only tools may be included

questions.explanation: Servers can include a tools array and optional toolChoice in a sampling request. The definitions are scoped to that request (they needn't match the server's own tools), but this is gated on the client declaring the sampling.tools capability.

questions.question: Put the MRTR flow in the correct order: (1) server returns InputRequiredResult, (2) client sends the initial request, (3) server returns a complete result, (4) client retries the original request with inputResponses and echoed requestState, (5) client gathers input from the user.
questions.explanation: Client sends the request; server answers resultType "input_required" with inputRequests and requestState; client gathers the answers; client retries the original request with inputResponses plus the echoed requestState; server completes. (Spec basic/patterns/mrtr.)

questions.question: On which client requests MAY a server return an InputRequiredResult?

options.text: Any request, including tools/list and server/discover
Only tools/call
prompts/get, resources/read, and tools/call - and servers MUST NOT send it on any other request
Only requests sent over Streamable HTTP

questions.explanation: The MRTR supported-requests table lists exactly prompts/get, resources/read, and tools/call. InputRequiredResult on anything else is a protocol violation. (Spec basic/patterns/mrtr, Supported Requests.)

questions.question: What kinds of request objects may appear as values in an InputRequiredResult's inputRequests map?

options.text: ElicitRequest, CreateMessageRequest (sampling), or ListRootsRequest
Any JSON-RPC request the server defines
Only ElicitRequest, since sampling and roots are removed
tools/call requests aimed back at the client

questions.explanation: inputRequests values MUST be one of ElicitRequest, CreateMessageRequest, or ListRootsRequest, keyed by server-assigned identifiers unique within the request. Sampling and roots are deprecated but still ride MRTR during the deprecation window - a favorite trap. (Spec basic/patterns/mrtr.)

questions.question: Which client behavior around requestState is compliant?

options.text: Base64-decode requestState to pre-fill the elicitation form
Echo the exact requestState value on the retry, without inspecting, parsing, or modifying it - and omit it entirely if the server sent none
Attach the requestState to a parallel tools/call to reuse the server's context
Cache requestState and reuse it for future unrelated requests to skip prompts

questions.explanation: requestState is opaque to clients: they MUST NOT inspect, parse, modify, or assume anything about it; MUST echo it exactly on the retry; MUST NOT include one if none was given; and MUST NOT use it for any other request. (Spec basic/patterns/mrtr, client requirements.)

questions.question: When a client retries the original request in an MRTR flow, what must be true of the JSON-RPC id?

options.text: It must be identical to the initial request's id so the server can correlate them
It must be null to mark it as a retry
It must be different from the initial request's id - the retry is an independent request
It must be the requestState value

questions.explanation: The initial request and the retry are completely independent requests, so the retry MUST use a different id. Correlation happens through the echoed requestState, not the JSON-RPC id. (Spec basic/patterns/mrtr, client requirements.)

questions.question: A server wants to return an InputRequiredResult that contains neither inputRequests nor requestState. Is that allowed?

options.text: Yes - both fields are optional
No - every InputRequiredResult MUST include at least one of inputRequests or requestState
Yes, but only on prompts/get
No - both fields are always required together

questions.explanation: Each field is individually optional, but the spec requires at least one of them in every InputRequiredResult; an empty one would give the client nothing to act on. (Spec basic/patterns/mrtr, server requirement 6.)

questions.question: A client's per-request capabilities do not declare elicitation. The server still needs user input to finish a tools/call. What may the server do?

options.text: Include an elicitation/create entry in inputRequests anyway - the client will figure it out
Fall back to a server-initiated elicitation/create request over the same stream
It MUST NOT include elicitation requests in inputRequests for that client; it can fail the request or complete without that input
Return resultType "task" to force the input later

questions.explanation: Servers MUST NOT send an inputRequests entry the client has not declared support for. Server-initiated requests no longer exist in the modern era, so the server must handle the request without elicitation or fail it. (Spec basic/patterns/mrtr, server requirement 7.)

questions.question: requestState passes through the client on every MRTR retry. What does the spec require of servers when this state influences authorization or business logic?

options.text: Nothing - clients are trusted to echo it faithfully

Treat it as attacker-controlled input: protect its integrity (e.g., HMAC or AEAD) and reject state that fails verification; bind principal, TTL, and originating request inside the protected payload to bound replay
Encrypt it with the client's public key
Store a copy server-side and compare on retry

questions.explanation: Servers MUST treat requestState as attacker-controlled. If it affects authorization, resource access, or business logic they MUST integrity-protect it and reject failures; they SHOULD embed the authenticated principal, a short TTL, and an identifier of the originating request. Single-use invariants still need server-side enforcement. (Spec basic/patterns/mrtr, server requirements 4-5.)

questions.question: A client's retry omits one of the answers the server asked for, and the server cannot proceed without it. What SHOULD the server do?

options.text: Return -32602 Invalid params
Return a new InputRequiredResult requesting the missing information again
Complete the request with default values
Close the connection to reset the flow

questions.explanation: If necessary information is missing, the server SHOULD respond with a fresh InputRequiredResult re-requesting it rather than erroring; unexpected extra fields in InputResponses are simply ignored. Servers may loop like this across multiple attempts. (Spec basic/patterns/mrtr, error handling.)

questions.question: Why does MRTR let stateless server fleets handle elicitation without sticky routing or shared storage?

options.text: Load balancers pin MRTR retries to the original instance via a cookie
The server encodes everything it needs into requestState, which the client echoes back - so any instance can reconstitute the state from the retry alone
The client stores the server's internal state in localStorage
MRTR requires a Redis-compatible shared cache

questions.explanation: The retry is self-contained: the instance handling it needs nothing beyond the request itself, because the prior context travels in the opaque requestState. That removes shared-storage and stateful load-balancing requirements. (Spec basic/patterns/mrtr, basic workflow.)

questions.question: An InputRequiredResult arrives carrying only requestState and no inputRequests. What may the client do?

options.text: Treat it as a protocol error
Retry the original request immediately, echoing the requestState
Prompt the user with a generic form
Send tasks/get to fetch the pending questions

questions.explanation: If inputRequests is absent the client MAY retry the original request immediately (with the echoed requestState). Only when inputRequests is present must the client construct the requested inputs first. (Spec basic/patterns/mrtr, client requirement 1.)

questions.question: Which resultType value marks an MRTR interim result?

options.text: "pending"
"input_required"
"task"
"incomplete"

questions.explanation: An InputRequiredResult is identified by resultType "input_required". "complete" is a normal final result and "task" belongs to the Tasks extension. (Spec basic/index, ResultType.)

questions.question: When building a STDIO-based MCP server, why must you never write log messages to stdout (e.g., with print() or console.log())?

options.text: stdout is reserved for the operating system
Writing to stdout corrupts the JSON-RPC messages and breaks the server
stdout output is too slow for logging
It exposes secrets to the user

questions.explanation: On the STDIO transport, stdout carries the JSON-RPC protocol messages, so any extra output corrupts them. Log to stderr instead (e.g., Python's logging module, console.error(), eprintln!()). For HTTP-based servers, stdout logging is fine.

questions.question: In which file do you register MCP servers for Claude for Desktop?

options.text: ~/.mcp/servers.yaml
claude_desktop_config.json, under the mcpServers key
package.json, under the mcp key
settings.ini in the install directory

questions.explanation: Servers are added to claude_desktop_config.json (on macOS at ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/) under the mcpServers key, each entry specifying the command and args used to launch the server.

questions.question: Why do the docs insist on absolute paths (not relative paths) in claude_desktop_config.json server entries?

options.text: Relative paths are rejected by the JSON parser
The working directory of a server launched by the client may be undefined (e.g., / on macOS), so relative paths resolve unpredictably
Absolute paths load faster
Relative paths only work on Windows

questions.explanation: Because the client could be started from anywhere, the spawned server's working directory may be undefined. Absolute paths in configuration and .env files ensure reliable operation.

questions.question: After editing claude_desktop_config.json, what must you do for the changes to take effect?

options.text: Nothing; the file is hot-reloaded
Fully quit and restart Claude for Desktop — simply closing the window is not enough
Run claude --reload from the terminal
Reboot the operating system

questions.explanation: You must fully quit the application (Cmd+Q on macOS, or Quit/Exit from the system tray on Windows) and reopen it. Closing the window does not fully quit the app, so the configuration changes will not be picked up.

questions.question: In the Python quickstart weather server, what does the MCPServer class use to automatically generate tool definitions?

options.text: A separate tools.yaml manifest
Python type hints and docstrings on the decorated functions
Reflection on function bytecode
A GUI-based schema editor

questions.explanation: The MCPServer class uses Python type hints and docstrings to automatically generate tool definitions, so a function decorated with @mcp.tool() gets its schema and description from its signature and docstring.

questions.question: When a user asks a question in an MCP host like Claude for Desktop, what is the correct order of events?

options.text: The server picks a tool, executes it, and sends the answer directly to the user

The client sends the question to the model; the model decides which tool(s) to use; the client executes them through the MCP server; results return to the model, which formulates the response shown to the user
The model connects directly to the MCP server over TCP and streams the answer
The user must manually invoke each tool before asking the question

questions.explanation: Under the hood: the client sends the question to the model, the model analyzes available tools and picks one or more, the client executes them via the MCP server, results go back to the model, and the model formulates the natural-language response.

questions.question: In the 'Build with Agent Skills' guide, which deployment path is the default recommendation for a server wrapping a cloud API?

options.text: Local stdio
Remote Streamable HTTP
An MCP Bundle (MCPB)
A browser extension

questions.explanation: Remote Streamable HTTP is the default for anything wrapping a cloud API: zero install friction, one deployment serves all users, and OAuth flows work properly since the server can handle redirects and token storage.

questions.question: What problem do MCP Bundles (MCPB) solve?

options.text: They compress protocol messages for slow networks
They package a local stdio server together with its runtime as a single .mcpb archive, so users can install it without setting up Node or Python
They bundle multiple remote servers behind one URL
They convert servers into browser apps

questions.explanation: MCPB packages a local server with its runtime as one .mcpb archive — the right path when the server must touch the user's machine (local files, desktop apps, localhost services) but users shouldn't need a dev environment.

questions.question: The reference mcp-server-dev plugin provides three composing skills. Which option lists them correctly?

options.text: build-mcp-server, build-mcp-app, build-mcpb
scaffold-server, test-server, deploy-server
mcp-init, mcp-auth, mcp-deploy
server-skill, client-skill, registry-skill

questions.explanation: The plugin ships build-mcp-server (the entry point that interrogates the use case), build-mcp-app (interactive UI widgets rendered in chat), and build-mcpb (packaging a local stdio server with its runtime).

questions.question: What are the system requirements for the Python weather-server quickstart?

options.text: Python 3.10 or higher and Python MCP SDK 2.0.0 or higher
Python 2.7 and any SDK version
Python 3.6 with pip only
Anaconda is mandatory

questions.explanation: The quickstart requires Python 3.10+ and the Python MCP SDK 2.0.0+, using uv to set up the project and install mcp[cli].

questions.question: In the TypeScript quickstart, which function is safe to use for logging in a STDIO server?

options.text: console.log()
console.error(), because it writes to stderr
process.stdout.write()
alert()

questions.explanation: console.log() writes to stdout and would corrupt the JSON-RPC stream; console.error() writes to stderr, which is safe (and is captured by hosts like Claude Desktop into the server's log file).

questions.question: SCENARIO: You added your new server to claude_desktop_config.json, restarted the window, but the server doesn't appear under Connectors. Which troubleshooting sequence matches the docs?

options.text: Reinstall the operating system
Check the config file's JSON syntax, make sure the server path is absolute (not relative), and fully quit Claude Desktop (Cmd+Q / tray Quit) before reopening — closing the window isn't a real restart
Switch the server to HTTP transport; stdio is unsupported in Claude Desktop
Rename the server to 'default'

questions.explanation: The troubleshooting guide lists exactly this: verify claude_desktop_config.json syntax, use absolute paths, and restart Claude Desktop completely. Logs in ~/Library/Logs/Claude (mcp.log, mcp-server-NAME.log) help diagnose further.

questions.question: SCENARIO: Your weather quickstart server returns 'Failed to retrieve grid point data' when asked about London. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The JSON-RPC id was a string instead of a number
The coordinates are outside the US — the server uses the US National Weather Service API, which only supports US locations
stdout logging corrupted the transport
The tool name contains an underscore

questions.explanation: The quickstart uses api.weather.gov (NWS), so only US locations work. The docs list non-US coordinates, NWS API outages, and rate limiting as the usual causes of this error.

questions.question: In the C# quickstart, why must you use Host.CreateEmptyApplicationBuilder instead of CreateDefaultBuilder for a STDIO server?

options.text: CreateDefaultBuilder is deprecated in .NET
CreateEmptyApplicationBuilder ensures the server writes no additional messages to the console, which would otherwise corrupt the STDIO protocol stream
It enables HTTPS by default
It is required for dependency injection

questions.explanation: The default builder writes startup messages to the console (stdout). For STDIO transport that would corrupt JSON-RPC messages, so the quickstart uses CreateEmptyApplicationBuilder. The same principle appears in Java (banner off) and other SDKs.

questions.question: SCENARIO: You ask an agent with the build-mcp-server skill installed to 'help me build an MCP server for our CRM'. What does the skill do before writing any code?

options.text: Immediately generates a random scaffold
Runs a short discovery phase asking what it connects to, who will use it, action surface size, user interaction needs, and upstream auth — then recommends a deployment path
Asks only for your API key
Downloads all reference servers

questions.explanation: The entry skill interrogates the use case first (connection target, audience, action surface, interaction needs, auth) and then recommends one of four deployment paths — remote Streamable HTTP, MCP apps, MCPB, or local stdio — skipping ahead if your opening message already covers the answers.

questions.question: In the build-client Python tutorial, what does the 'async with Client(...)' block represent?

options.text: Only a timeout wrapper
The entire connection lifecycle: entering it launches the server subprocess and agrees a protocol version; leaving it disconnects and shuts the subprocess down
A database transaction
A retry loop for failed queries

questions.explanation: The tutorial stresses there is no connect/close pair to call: the async with block owns the whole lifecycle — launch, version agreement, and clean shutdown — with nothing to close by hand.

questions.question: In the client tutorial, how should your code detect that a tool call failed?

options.text: Wrap call_tool in try/except; failing tools always raise
Check result.is_error — a tool that raises on the server does not raise in the client; it answers with is_error set, and passing that flag to the model lets it read the message and try something else
Check for an HTTP 500 status
Compare the output against an empty string

questions.explanation: CallToolResult carries content blocks plus an is_error flag. The best-practices section says explicitly: check result.is_error rather than expecting a failing tool to raise.

questions.question: SCENARIO: A user submits a query to your MCP-powered chatbot client. Which sequence of steps does the tutorial describe?

options.text: The server answers the user directly, bypassing the model

Client fetches the tool list from the server → sends the query plus tool descriptions to Claude → Claude decides which tools to use → client executes them through the server → results go back to Claude → Claude produces the natural-language response shown to the user
Claude connects to the MCP server directly over stdio
The user must pick a tool manually before typing the query

questions.explanation: This seven-step flow (list tools, send with query, model decides, client executes via server, results back, model responds, display) is the core loop every quickstart client implements.

questions.question: SCENARIO: Your new client connects to the weather server but the very first response takes ~25 seconds, and a teammate suggests killing the process. Per the troubleshooting guidance, what's correct?

options.text: Anything over 5 seconds indicates a broken transport
The first response can take up to 30 seconds while the server initializes, Claude processes the query, and tools execute; subsequent responses are faster — don't interrupt the initial waiting period
Restart the OS networking stack
Switch the model to a smaller one to fix startup time

questions.explanation: The troubleshooting section notes the first response may take up to 30 seconds (server init + model processing + tool execution) and that this is normal; later responses are typically faster.

questions.question: Why does the Python client tutorial run input() via asyncio.to_thread in the chat loop?

options.text: input() is deprecated in Python 3.10
input() blocks, so running it on a worker thread keeps the event loop free to service the MCP connection while the user types
To capture keystrokes for autocomplete
Threads are required for stdout logging

questions.explanation: Because input() is blocking, calling it directly would stall the asyncio event loop and the connection with it; asyncio.to_thread moves it to a worker thread.

questions.question: What problem does progressive tool discovery solve for MCP hosts connected to many servers?

options.text: Slow network transports
Loading every tool definition into the model's context upfront wastes tokens, adds latency, and degrades model performance
Servers refusing to list their tools
OAuth token expiry

questions.explanation: With hundreds of tools, upfront definitions can consume most of the context window. Progressive discovery defers injecting definitions, exposing a lightweight search_tools meta-tool and loading full definitions only as needed.

questions.question: In the three-layer progressive discovery pattern, what are the layers?

options.text: Catalog, Inspect, Execute
Search, Sort, Send
List, Cache, Call
Discover, Authorize, Invoke

questions.explanation: Layer 1 (Catalog): a search_tools meta-tool returns matching names with brief descriptions. Layer 2 (Inspect): the model fetches the full definition of only the tool it needs. Layer 3 (Execute): the model calls the tool with full knowledge of its interface.

questions.question: What threshold do the docs recommend for switching from loading all tools to progressive discovery?

options.text: When more than 100 servers are connected
When tool definitions consume roughly 1%–5% of the context window
When any single tool schema exceeds 1 MB
Progressive discovery should always be used, regardless of size

questions.explanation: For a small tool set, loading everything is fine. Clients should implement a threshold as a percentage of the context window — for example 1%–5% — and switch to progressive discovery once tool definitions cross it.

questions.question: What is 'programmatic tool calling' (code mode)?

options.text: The model writes code that calls tools; the code runs in a sandbox and only the final result returns to the model
Tools written exclusively in Python
A mode where the server executes tools without client approval
Pre-compiling tool schemas to WebAssembly

questions.explanation: Instead of round-tripping every intermediate result through the model's context, the model writes a script against typed APIs generated from MCP tool schemas. The sandbox executes it, intermediate data flows between servers via the host broker, and only e.g. a console.log summary returns to the model.

questions.question: In a code-mode architecture, which statement about credentials and network access is correct?

options.text: The sandbox holds API keys so tool calls are faster
The sandbox should have no direct network access; credentials are held by the host broker, which adds authentication when forwarding calls to servers
The model receives all tokens so it can decide which to use
Each MCP server pushes its credentials into the sandbox at startup

questions.explanation: The sandbox is isolated: its only interface is the generated function stubs that route back to the host. The host acts as broker, holds authorization tokens, enforces per-call authorization, and never exposes credentials to model-generated code.

questions.question: How should generated code-mode wrappers handle an MCP tool response with isError: true?

options.text: Ignore it, since the transport succeeded
Convert it into a thrown exception so model-authored code can use try/catch
Retry the call automatically up to 10 times
Terminate the sandbox immediately without reporting

questions.explanation: MCP tool errors arrive as successful responses with isError: true, not transport failures. Wrappers should convert this into a thrown exception; if an uncaught error ends the script, surface it as the script's result so the model can self-correct.

questions.question: Which of these is a recommended implementation guideline for progressive discovery?

options.text: Re-fetch tools/list from the server every time a definition is needed
Cache tool definitions host-side once fetched, and re-index the search catalog when a notifications/tools/list_changed arrives
Hide the source server of each tool from the model
Only ever expose one tool at a time

questions.explanation: Guidelines include offering multiple detail levels, caching definitions host-side, refreshing the catalog on list_changed notifications, and grouping tools by server so the model can reason about related capabilities.

questions.question: Why can adding or removing tool definitions mid-conversation be costly even when it saves definition tokens?

options.text: Servers charge per tools/list call
It invalidates the provider's prompt cache (which includes the tools array), and the resulting cache miss can cost more tokens than the definitions removed
It forces the client to reconnect to every server
JSON-RPC requires renumbering all message IDs

questions.explanation: Most providers cache the prompt prefix including the tools array. To preserve caching, append newly discovered definitions after the cache breakpoint or route calls through a single stable call_tool meta-tool, and treat server disconnection as a conversation-boundary operation.

questions.question: In progressive discovery, what does the lightweight search_tools meta-tool return?

options.text: Full JSON Schemas for every tool on every server
Concise matches: tool names and one-line descriptions only
Executable code for each tool
A ranked list of servers to disconnect

questions.explanation: The catalog layer returns only names and brief descriptions (e.g., salesforce_updateRecord — 'Update fields on a Salesforce object'); the model then inspects the full definition of just the tool it needs.

questions.question: What is the main drawback of direct tool calling when chaining multiple tools together?

options.text: Tools cannot be chained at all
Every intermediate result flows through the model's context, consuming tokens and adding latency even when the model doesn't need it
It requires OAuth for every call
It only works over stdio
