questions.explanation: With direct calling, each invocation is a round trip through the model. Programmatic tool calling (code mode) fixes this by letting data flow between servers inside a sandbox, with only the final summary returning to the model.

questions.question: Under dynamic server management, what can a host do instead of connecting to every configured server at startup?

options.text: Nothing; all servers must connect at startup
Keep a registry of available servers, connect to a server only when the model needs its capabilities, and disconnect servers no longer relevant to free context
Merge all servers into one process
Randomly sample three servers per conversation

questions.explanation: Progressive discovery extends to whole servers: maintain a registry with high-level descriptions, connect on demand (e.g., enable_server('salesforce')), and disconnect when done. This suits general-purpose agents where intent isn't known upfront.

questions.question: Which discovery strategies do the docs list for implementing search_tools?

options.text: Keyword-based, embedding-based, subagent-based, and hybrid approaches
Alphabetical sorting only
Random selection with retries
Manual user selection for every call

questions.explanation: Options include keyword matching (BM25/regex), vector-similarity embeddings, a small fast subagent model (e.g., Claude Haiku) selecting tools, or hybrids. Some providers (OpenAI, Anthropic) offer built-in tool search you may prefer.

questions.question: SCENARIO: A task requires reading thousands of error log entries, deduplicating them, and filing one ticket per unique error. Which approach keeps the log data out of the model's context?

options.text: Direct tool calling with the full log dump returned to the model each time

Code mode: the model writes a script that calls logging_getLogs, filters and deduplicates inside the sandbox, calls ticketing_createIssue per unique error, and returns only a one-line console.log summary
Asking the user to paste the logs manually
Increasing the model's max tokens

questions.explanation: This is the canonical code-mode example: log data and ticket creation flow between servers through the host broker without entering the model's context; only the summary line (e.g., 'Filed 7 tickets from 3,214 error logs') returns.

questions.question: SCENARIO: A user approves a code-mode script that will call ticketing_createIssue in a loop. Mid-run, the script tries to call payments_transferFunds, which the user never discussed. What does the security guidance say the host broker should do?

options.text: Allow it — approving the script grants blanket approval for all runtime calls
Evaluate each sandbox-originated call against the granted approval: script approval is not blanket approval, so a call outside the grant (like payments_transferFunds) requires its own authorization
Kill the sandbox and delete all tickets already created
Log it silently and continue

questions.explanation: Per-call authorization: the broker is still the MCP host for spec purposes. Hosts may grant categorical approval (e.g., 'allow ticketing_createIssue for this run') rather than prompting per iteration, but every call must still be evaluated against that grant — approving the script does not approve everything it might do.

questions.question: When a tool provides no outputSchema, what does the guidance recommend for typing its results in code mode?

options.text: Refuse to call the tool

Prefer a generic type (any/string) and handle unstructured output downstream; optionally use a host-brokered extract(value, ExpectedType) helper backed by a fast model for single-shot calls, validating the result before use
Guess the schema from the tool's name
Always regenerate the whole API from scratch

questions.explanation: The simple path is a generic type — the real fix is server authors providing outputSchema. An extract() helper routed through the host (never giving the sandbox network access) can coerce values via a small model, but it adds latency and can hallucinate, so validate against the expected type.

questions.question: MCP's authorization model follows the conventions of which framework?

options.text: SAML 2.0
OAuth 2.1
Kerberos
Basic authentication over HTTPS

questions.explanation: MCP authorization follows OAuth 2.1 conventions (authorization code flow with PKCE), building on standards like RFC 8414 (auth server metadata), RFC 7591 (dynamic client registration), RFC 9728 (protected resource metadata), and RFC 8707 (resource indicators).

questions.question: When an unauthenticated client first contacts a protected MCP server, how does the server kick off the authorization flow?

options.text: It returns 200 with a login form
It responds 401 Unauthorized with a WWW-Authenticate header whose resource_metadata parameter points to the Protected Resource Metadata document
It silently drops the connection
It redirects the client to google.com/oauth

questions.explanation: The server answers 401 and the WWW-Authenticate header carries resource_metadata, pointing to the PRM document (RFC 9728) at a well-known path. The client fetches it to learn the authorization server(s), supported scopes, and resource information.

questions.question: What is Dynamic Client Registration (DCR) used for in MCP authorization?

options.text: Registering new tools at runtime
Allowing an MCP client to register itself with an authorization server on the fly, instead of being pre-registered
Registering the MCP server in the public registry
Rotating TLS certificates

questions.explanation: With DCR (RFC 7591), the client posts its information (name, redirect URIs, grant types) to the authorization server's registration_endpoint and receives client registration details, avoiding manual pre-registration. If neither DCR nor pre-registration is available, the client should let the user enter client information manually.

questions.question: Why is validating the aud (audience) claim of an access token critical for an MCP server?

options.text: It determines the token's encryption algorithm
It verifies the token was actually issued for this MCP server, preventing token reuse across services and token passthrough scenarios
It contains the user's display name
It sets the token's expiry time

questions.explanation: The audience embeds the intended destination in the token. Checking that aud matches the MCP server's resource prevents accepting tokens minted for other APIs — a key defense against the token passthrough anti-pattern.

questions.question: According to the authorization tutorial, when is OAuth-based authorization typically NOT necessary for an MCP server?

options.text: When the server is hosted in the cloud
When the server uses the STDIO transport locally — it can use environment-based credentials instead
When the server has fewer than five tools
When users are on the same corporate network

questions.explanation: OAuth flows are designed for HTTP-based transports with remotely hosted servers. Local STDIO servers can use environment-based credentials or credentials from embedded libraries, since they run on the user's machine.

questions.question: Once the OAuth flow completes, how does an MCP client authenticate requests to the MCP server?

options.text: By appending ?token=... to every URL
By sending the access token in the Authorization: Bearer header
By embedding the token in the JSON-RPC id field
By client TLS certificates only

questions.explanation: The client includes the access token in the Authorization header as a Bearer token; the server must validate the token (e.g., via introspection or JWT validation) before processing the request.

questions.question: Which of the following is listed as an authorization pitfall to avoid?

options.text: Using well-tested libraries for token validation
Using short-lived access tokens
Logging Authorization headers and tokens for easier debugging
Returning WWW-Authenticate challenges on 401

questions.explanation: Never log credentials: no Authorization headers, tokens, codes, or secrets; scrub query strings and redact sensitive fields. The other options are recommended practices, not pitfalls.

questions.question: Which RFC defines the Protected Resource Metadata document used in MCP authorization discovery?

options.text: RFC 9728
RFC 2616
RFC 6455
RFC 791

questions.explanation: RFC 9728 defines Protected Resource Metadata. Related standards: RFC 8414 (Authorization Server Metadata), RFC 7591 (Dynamic Client Registration), and RFC 8707 (Resource Indicators).

questions.question: Is authorization mandatory for MCP servers?

options.text: Yes, every MCP server must implement OAuth
No — it's optional, but strongly recommended when the server accesses user-specific data, needs auditing, requires user consent, targets enterprises, or needs per-user rate limiting
Only remote servers are allowed to have authorization
Authorization is decided by the model at runtime

questions.explanation: Authorization is optional in MCP, but strongly recommended for servers handling user data, auditable actions, consent-gated APIs, enterprise access controls, or per-user rate limiting/usage tracking.

questions.question: After the user consents at the authorization endpoint, what does the client exchange the authorization code for?

options.text: A username and password
Tokens — an access token (and typically a refresh token) returned with token_type and expires_in
A client certificate
A session cookie for the MCP server

questions.explanation: The authorization server redirects back with an authorization code, which the client exchanges at the token endpoint for an access token (plus refresh token, token_type Bearer, expires_in), following standard OAuth 2.1 authorization code with PKCE.

questions.question: Which OAuth extension does MCP's authorization code flow use to protect the code exchange?

options.text: PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange)
SAML assertions
HTTP Digest authentication
Kerberos tickets

questions.explanation: The user authorization step follows standard OAuth 2.1 authorization code with PKCE conventions, which protects the authorization code exchange against interception.

questions.question: SCENARIO: Your MCP server at http://localhost:3000 introspects a token and finds aud: ["account", "test-client"] — neither matching your server's resource. The token is otherwise valid and unexpired. What should your server do?

options.text: Accept it; the token is valid and active
Reject the request — none of the audiences match the configured resource, so the token was not issued for this server
Accept it but log a warning
Forward the token to the downstream API to let it decide

questions.explanation: The tutorial's verifier does exactly this: it checks each audience against the server's resource URL and rejects when none match. Accepting foreign-audience tokens is the token passthrough anti-pattern.

questions.question: In the Keycloak tutorial, how does the example MCP server verify that a received token is valid?

options.text: By comparing it to a hardcoded string
Via OAuth 2.0 Token Introspection (RFC 7662) against Keycloak's introspection endpoint (JWT validation via libraries is an equally valid alternative)
By asking the MCP client to vouch for it
Tokens are trusted implicitly over localhost

questions.explanation: The sample servers post the token to Keycloak's introspection endpoint using the server's own client credentials, checking active, scope, expiry, and audience. The docs note introspection is one of several valid approaches — standalone JWT-validation libraries work too.

questions.question: SCENARIO: Your MCP client connects to a server whose authorization server does not support Dynamic Client Registration, and your client is not pre-registered with it. What does the tutorial say is the client developer's responsibility?

options.text: Refuse to connect permanently
Provide an affordance for the end user to enter client registration information manually
Generate a random client_id and hope it works
Fall back to sending no credentials

questions.explanation: When neither DCR nor pre-registration is available, it's the client developer's responsibility to let the end user enter client information manually so the flow can still complete.

questions.question: Why should MCP servers 'return proper challenges' on a 401?

options.text: To satisfy HTTP/2 framing rules
Including WWW-Authenticate with Bearer, realm, and resource_metadata lets clients discover how to authenticate automatically
To trigger the browser's basic-auth popup
Challenges are only needed on 500 errors

questions.explanation: The 401 challenge is the entry point of the whole discovery chain: without WWW-Authenticate carrying resource_metadata (and optionally required scopes), the client can't find the PRM document or the authorization server and the flow can't start.

questions.question: SCENARIO: Match the HTTP status a protected MCP server should return: (1) request with no token or an invalid/expired token; (2) valid token lacking a required scope; (3) request whose Mcp-Name header contradicts the body.

options.text: (1) 401 Unauthorized with a WWW-Authenticate challenge; (2) 403 with insufficient_scope (triggering step-up); (3) 400 Bad Request with the HeaderMismatch error
All three return 401

questions.explanation: 401 means authenticate (the WWW-Authenticate header kicks off discovery); 403 insufficient_scope means the identity is known but lacks permission, prompting step-up authorization for additional scopes; 400 + HeaderMismatch (-32020) covers malformed requests whose headers and body disagree.

questions.question: After a 403 insufficient_scope challenge, which scopes should the client request when re-authorizing?

options.text: Only the newly challenged scopes, discarding old ones
The union of previously granted scopes and the newly challenged scopes, so the new token covers everything the old one did plus the new requirement
All scopes in scopes_supported, always
No scopes; scopes are server-side only

questions.explanation: Scope accumulation is a client-side responsibility in the step-up flow: compute the union of held and challenged scopes so previously granted permissions aren't lost, while servers stay stateless about client scope sets.

questions.question: SCENARIO: A client connects to a brand-new protected server and receives 401 with WWW-Authenticate but NO scope parameter. Per the scope selection strategy, what should it request?

options.text: No scopes at all
Fall back to requesting all scopes listed in the PRM document's scopes_supported, letting the authorization server and end user decide during consent
Invent scopes based on tool names
Abort the connection

questions.explanation: When the initial challenge carries no scope parameter, the documented fallback is to request everything in scopes_supported — general-purpose MCP clients lack domain knowledge to pick, so the authorization server and user determine appropriate permissions at consent time.

questions.question: What is the 'token passthrough' anti-pattern?

options.text: Forwarding refresh tokens over plain HTTP
An MCP server accepting tokens from a client without validating they were issued to the MCP server, and forwarding them to a downstream API
Storing tokens in a database
Re-using one PKCE verifier across flows

questions.explanation: Token passthrough is explicitly forbidden: MCP servers MUST NOT accept tokens that were not explicitly issued for them. Accepting and forwarding foreign-audience tokens circumvents security controls, breaks audit trails, and creates confused deputy risks.

questions.question: Which combination of conditions enables the confused deputy attack against an MCP proxy server?

options.text: HTTPS everywhere, short-lived tokens, and PKCE
A static client ID with the third-party auth server, dynamic client registration for MCP clients, a consent cookie set after first authorization, and no per-client consent at the proxy
Rate limiting combined with token rotation
Using JWTs instead of opaque tokens

questions.explanation: When the proxy uses one static client ID upstream, allows clients to register dynamically, and the third-party server skips consent because of a cookie, an attacker can register a malicious redirect URI and steal authorization codes. The mitigation is mandatory per-client consent before forwarding to third-party authorization.

questions.question: During OAuth metadata discovery, why should server-deployed MCP clients block requests to addresses like http://169.254.169.254/?

options.text: That range is reserved for IPv6 tunneling
It is the cloud metadata endpoint; a malicious server could use SSRF via crafted metadata URLs to exfiltrate cloud credentials
Requests to it are always rate-limited
It only serves IPv4 traffic

questions.explanation: A malicious MCP server can point resource_metadata or authorization endpoints at internal resources. 169.254.169.254 is the AWS/GCP/Azure metadata service, which can leak IAM credentials — one reason clients should enforce HTTPS, block private/link-local IP ranges, validate redirects, and consider egress proxies.

questions.question: Since MCP 2026-07-28 is stateless, servers that need multi-request state mint explicit state handles (e.g., a cart ID). What is the core mitigation against state handle hijacking?

options.text: Encrypting the handle with the client's public key
Never treating possession of a handle as authentication: verify every request, use secure random handles, and bind handles server-side to the authenticated user
Making handles sequential so they are easy to audit
Embedding the handle in the URL path

questions.explanation: Servers MUST verify all inbound requests and MUST NOT treat handle possession as authentication. Handles should be non-deterministic, ideally expiring, and bound server-side (e.g., keyed as user_id:handle from the verified token) so a guessed handle can't be used by another principal.

questions.question: Which URL schemes may an MCP client accept for OAuth authorization URLs?

options.text: Any scheme, as long as the URL is well-formed
Only http:// and https:// — with http restricted to loopback addresses during development; javascript:, data:, file:, and vbscript: must be rejected
https:// and ftp://
Custom app schemes like myapp:// only

questions.explanation: Malicious servers can supply javascript: URLs (XSS) or shell-injection payloads. Clients MUST allowlist http/https only (http only for loopback in development), MUST NOT open URLs via shell commands, and should sanitize all URLs received from servers.

questions.question: What must an MCP client do before executing a one-click local MCP server configuration?

options.text: Nothing, if the server comes from the official registry
Show the exact, untruncated command to be executed, identify it as potentially dangerous, and require explicit user approval
Run the command once in dry-run mode
Upload the command to a virus scanner

questions.explanation: Because local servers can execute arbitrary code with the client's privileges, one-click configuration MUST show the exact command (with arguments), clearly flag the risk, require explicit approval, and allow cancellation. Sandboxing and dangerous-pattern warnings are additionally recommended.

questions.question: What scope design does the security guidance recommend for MCP servers?

options.text: One omnibus scope like full-access to minimize consent dialogs
A progressive, least-privilege model: minimal initial scopes, with incremental elevation via targeted WWW-Authenticate scope challenges when privileged operations are attempted
Wildcard scopes per department
No scopes at all; rely on network isolation

questions.explanation: Broad up-front scopes expand blast radius and obscure audit trails. The recommendation is minimal initial scopes (e.g., mcp:tools-basic), step-up authorization via precise scope challenges, and client-side accumulation of the union of granted and newly challenged scopes.

questions.question: According to the spec's Security and Trust & Safety principles, what must happen before a host invokes any tool?

options.text: The tool must be signed by Anthropic
The host must obtain explicit user consent, and users should understand what the tool does
The server must pass a benchmark suite
The tool must run once in a simulator

questions.explanation: Tools represent arbitrary code execution. Hosts must obtain explicit user consent before invoking any tool, tool descriptions/annotations should be treated as untrusted unless from a trusted server, and users must retain control over data sharing and actions.

questions.question: Should you write your own token validation and authorization logic from scratch for an MCP server?

options.text: Yes, custom code is always more secure
No — use off-the-shelf, well-tested libraries; implementing it yourself makes mistakes far more likely unless you're a security expert
Only if the server is written in Rust
Token validation is optional

questions.explanation: The guidance is explicit: do not implement token validation or authorization logic yourself. Use well-tested, secure libraries for token validation and authorization decisions.

questions.question: When is plain http:// acceptable for OAuth-related MCP URLs?

options.text: Whenever the server is behind a firewall
Only for loopback addresses (localhost, 127.0.0.1, ::1) during development; production must use HTTPS
Always, since tokens are already encrypted
Never, not even for localhost

questions.explanation: HTTPS must be enforced in production. The only exception is loopback addresses during local development — aligning with OAuth 2.1's requirement of HTTPS for all protocol URLs except loopback redirects.

questions.question: Why does the security guidance recommend short-lived access tokens?

options.text: They are smaller and faster to parse
If a malicious actor steals a token, a short lifetime limits how long they can maintain access
Authorization servers charge per token-hour
Long-lived tokens are not valid JSON

questions.explanation: Short-lived tokens shrink the window of usefulness for stolen credentials. Combined with secure encrypted storage and cache eviction of expired tokens, this limits the blast radius of a leak.

questions.question: Which of these should NEVER appear in your MCP server's logs?

options.text: Request timing and correlation IDs
Authorization headers, tokens, authorization codes, and secrets
Tool names being invoked
Error patterns

questions.explanation: Never log credentials: no Authorization headers, tokens, codes, or secrets. Scrub query strings and headers, and redact sensitive fields in structured logs. Timing, correlation IDs, tool executions, and error patterns are exactly what you should log.

questions.question: SCENARIO: A client sends your MCP server a syntactically valid, unexpired JWT originally issued for a company's calendar API. Your server forwards it to its downstream API, which accepts it. What have you just implemented?

options.text: Federated single sign-on, which is encouraged
The forbidden token passthrough anti-pattern — the server accepted a token not issued for it and forwarded it, circumventing security controls and breaking audit trails
Correct OAuth 2.1 behavior
Resource indicator negotiation

questions.explanation: MCP servers MUST NOT accept tokens not explicitly issued for them. Passing them through bypasses rate limiting and validation, makes logs attribute requests to the wrong identity, and can turn the server into a data-exfiltration proxy.

questions.question: SCENARIO: A user previously authorized your MCP proxy against a third-party API. Weeks later, they click a link from an attacker; the third-party auth server sees its old consent cookie for your static client ID, skips the consent screen, and the authorization code lands on the attacker's redirect URI (registered via DCR). Which mitigation would have stopped this?

options.text: Longer-lived consent cookies

The proxy implementing per-client consent — maintaining a registry of approved client_ids per user and showing its own consent page BEFORE forwarding to third-party authorization, plus strict exact-match redirect URI validation
Switching from OAuth to API keys
Using GET instead of POST for the token exchange

questions.explanation: This is the confused deputy attack. The mitigation: per-client consent storage checked before initiating third-party authorization, an MCP-level consent page identifying the client and redirect_uri, CSRF-protected state handling, and exact-string redirect URI matching.

questions.question: SCENARIO: Your stateless MCP shopping server mints cart handles as sequential integers (cart-1041, cart-1042, ...) and any request presenting a handle can modify that cart. An attacker increments the number and edits another user's cart. Which two fixes does the guidance require/recommend?

options.text: Rate limiting alone

Verify authorization on every inbound request (never treat handle possession as authentication), and use secure non-deterministic handles bound server-side to the authenticated user (e.g., keyed as user_id:handle from the verified token)
Encode the handle in base64
Move the handle to a custom HTTP header

questions.explanation: State handle hijacking mitigations: servers MUST verify all requests and MUST NOT treat handle possession as authentication; handles SHOULD be securely random (ideally expiring) and bound server-side to the verified user so even a guessed handle is rejected for other principals.

questions.question: Which key principles does the specification's 'Security and Trust & Safety' section define?

options.text: User Consent and Control, Data Privacy, and Tool Safety (earlier revisions also listed LLM Sampling Controls as a fourth, before sampling's deprecation)
Speed, Scale, and Simplicity
Encryption, Compression, and Caching
Availability, Latency, and Throughput

questions.explanation: The 2026-07-28 spec lists User Consent and Control (explicit consent for all data access and operations), Data Privacy (hosts must not transmit resource data without consent), and Tool Safety (tools are arbitrary code; descriptions are untrusted unless from a trusted server). Pre-2026 revisions included LLM Sampling Controls as a fourth principle.

questions.question: SCENARIO: Your MCP server's JWT validator checks signature, expiry, and issuer — but not the aud claim. A partner service's leaked token (valid, same issuer, audience 'https://billing.internal') is replayed against your server. What happens, and what's the fix?

options.text: Nothing happens; the issuer check is sufficient

The token is accepted despite being minted for another service — an audience validation failure. Fix: verify the aud claim matches your server's resource identifier and reject all others, per the token passthrough prohibition
The token is rejected because JWTs are single-use
TLS prevents this attack entirely

questions.explanation: Audience validation failure is one of token passthrough's two critical dimensions: same-issuer tokens for other resources must be rejected. Servers MUST NOT accept tokens not explicitly issued for them — signature/expiry/issuer checks alone don't establish the token was meant for you.

questions.question: Which combination of conditions makes an MCP proxy server vulnerable to the confused deputy attack?

options.text: PKCE enabled + short-lived tokens + refresh rotation
Static client ID at the third-party AS + dynamic client registration for MCP clients + a consent cookie set after first authorization + no per-client consent at the proxy
Wildcard scopes + long-lived refresh tokens
stdio transport + unsandboxed subprocesses

questions.explanation: All four conditions together let an attacker register a malicious client with their own redirect_uri, reuse the victim's consent cookie (set for the proxy's static client ID), skip the consent screen, and receive the authorization code. (Security Best Practices, Confused Deputy.)

questions.question: What is the required mitigation for the confused deputy problem in MCP proxy servers?

options.text: Rotate the static client ID daily
Per-client consent: keep a registry of approved client_id values per user and check it BEFORE forwarding to the third-party authorization flow
Disable dynamic client registration entirely
Use longer authorization codes

questions.explanation: Proxies MUST implement per-client consent that runs before the third-party flow, storing decisions bound to the specific client_id - never trusting a consent cookie that reflects a different client. The consent UI must show the client name, scopes, and redirect_uri. (Security Best Practices, Confused Deputy mitigation.)

questions.question: For an MCP proxy's OAuth flow, when must the state-tracking cookie or session be set, and why?

options.text: Before showing the consent screen, so the state survives a refresh
Immediately before redirecting to the third-party IdP, and only AFTER the user approved consent - otherwise an attacker can bypass the consent screen with a crafted request
After the token exchange completes
State cookies are forbidden; use localStorage

questions.explanation: Setting the state cookie before consent approval renders the consent screen ineffective. State values must also be cryptographically random, single-use, short-lived, and validated exactly at the callback. (Security Best Practices, OAuth state parameter validation.)

questions.question: Why is token passthrough forbidden for MCP servers?

options.text: It doubles token size on the wire

Accepting tokens not issued to the MCP server (wrong audience) breaks OAuth boundaries, bypasses rate limiting and audit controls, and lets the server be used as a proxy for exfiltration - servers MUST NOT accept tokens not explicitly issued for them
It only works with opaque tokens, not JWTs
It requires dynamic client registration, which is deprecated

questions.explanation: The two failure dimensions are audience-validation failure and forwarding unvalidated tokens downstream, which creates confused-deputy trust problems, breaks accountability/audit trails, and circumvents security controls. (Security Best Practices, Token Passthrough.)

questions.question: During OAuth discovery, which attacker-controllable inputs create SSRF risk for an MCP client?

options.text: Only the token endpoint URL
The resource_metadata URL from WWW-Authenticate, the authorization_servers URLs in Protected Resource Metadata, and endpoint URLs in Authorization Server Metadata
The JSON-RPC id field
The Mcp-Method header

questions.explanation: A malicious server controls all three discovery inputs and can point them at internal IPs, localhost services, or the 169.254.169.254 cloud metadata endpoint - the client then fetches them. (Security Best Practices, SSRF attack description.)

questions.question: Which SSRF mitigation set matches the guidance for server-deployed MCP clients?

options.text: Allow http:// everywhere but log each request

Require HTTPS except loopback during development; block private/reserved ranges (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, 127/8, 169.254/16 incl. metadata endpoints, fc00::/7, fe80::/10); avoid hand-rolled IP validation; validate redirect hops; consider egress proxies and DNS pinning against TOCTOU
Resolve DNS once at startup and cache forever
Only fetch metadata over HTTP/2

questions.explanation: This is the full mitigation list. Manual IP parsing is explicitly discouraged because attackers exploit octal/hex/IPv4-mapped-IPv6 encodings; DNS rebinding creates time-of-check/time-of-use gaps; egress proxies like Smokescreen block internal destinations by design. (Security Best Practices, SSRF mitigation.)

questions.question: An attacker guesses another user's shopping-cart handle and passes it as a tool argument. What server design defeats this state-handle hijacking?

options.text: Treat possession of the handle as proof of identity for speed

Never treat handle possession as authentication: verify the bearer token on every request, mint non-deterministic random handles, and bind state server-side as <user_id>:<handle> where user_id comes from the verified token
Use sequential integer handles so collisions are detectable
Embed the user's password inside the handle

questions.explanation: Servers MUST NOT treat a state handle as authentication and MUST verify all inbound requests. Random, expiring handles plus server-side binding to the authenticated principal mean a guessed handle is useless to another caller. (Security Best Practices, State Handle Hijacking.)

questions.question: A client offers one-click installation of a local MCP server from a link. Which consent behavior does the spec REQUIRE before executing anything?

options.text: Show a spinner while installing to avoid alarming the user
Display the exact, untruncated command with all arguments, identify it as a potentially dangerous operation that executes code, require explicit approval, and let the user cancel
Only require consent when the command contains sudo
Run the command in a VM first and show the output

questions.explanation: These four are the MUSTs for one-click local server configuration. SHOULDs add highlighting dangerous patterns (sudo, rm -rf), warning on sensitive paths, and sandboxing spawned servers. (Security Best Practices, Local MCP Server Compromise.)

questions.question: A malicious server returns javascript:alert(document.cookie) as its OAuth authorization URL. Which client rules prevent the resulting XSS/RCE class of attacks?

options.text: Open the URL in a private browsing window
Allow only http(s) schemes (http solely for loopback in development), reject javascript:/data:/file:/vbscript:, and never open URLs via shell commands - use non-shell platform mechanisms
URL-encode the value before opening it
Only open URLs shorter than 2048 characters

questions.explanation: Clients MUST validate authorization URL schemes with an allowlist and MUST NOT shell out to open URLs (shell interpretation enables command injection). Combined with a proxy architecture, such XSS can escalate to full RCE via stdio process spawning. (Security Best Practices, OAuth Authorization URL Validation.)

questions.question: A client holding scopes [read:files] gets 403 insufficient_scope with scope="write:files" when calling a privileged tool. What should it request when re-authorizing, and why?

options.text: Only write:files - minimal privilege means dropping old scopes
The union of previously requested and newly challenged scopes (read:files write:files), so previously granted permissions are not lost while the server stays stateless about client scope sets
All scopes in scopes_supported, to avoid future prompts
An admin scope that implies both

questions.explanation: Scope accumulation is a client-side responsibility: clients SHOULD compute the union of prior and challenged scopes on step-up. Requesting only the new scope loses existing grants; requesting the full catalog is the scope-inflation anti-pattern (wildcards, bundling, publishing everything in scopes_supported). (Security Best Practices, Scope Minimization.)

questions.question: The MCP Inspector ships as a single package with three clients. Which are they?

options.text: Web, CLI, and TUI
Desktop, Mobile, and Web
GUI, REPL, and Daemon
Chrome, Firefox, and Safari extensions

questions.explanation: @modelcontextprotocol/inspector provides three clients behind one binary: the Web UI (default), the CLI (--cli, scriptable for CI and agents), and the TUI (--tui, an interactive terminal UI). All share the same core, transports, config files, and OAuth state.

questions.question: How do you launch the MCP Inspector against a local stdio server without installing anything globally?

options.text: pip install mcp-inspector && mcp-inspector
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector node path/to/server/index.js
docker run mcp/inspector
cargo install inspector && inspector serve

questions.explanation: The Inspector runs directly through npx (requiring Node 22.19.0+). The command prints a URL containing a one-time session token to open in the browser.

questions.question: Which flags does the mcp-inspector launcher itself own?

options.text: All flags; it validates everything before forwarding
Only the mode flag (--web/--cli/--tui) and -h/--help; everything else is defined by the selected client
--method and --format
--catalog and --config

questions.explanation: The launcher is thin: it owns the mode flag and help. Mode flags are recognized only at the front of the command line; the first unowned token ends launcher parsing and everything after it is forwarded to the client unchanged.

questions.question: What is the key difference between the Inspector's --catalog and --config flags?

options.text: --catalog is for HTTP servers and --config is for stdio servers
--catalog is a writable server list (created and seeded if missing, default ~/.mcp-inspector/mcp.json); --config is read-only, never written, and errors if the file is missing
They are aliases of each other
--config can be combined with --catalog to merge lists

questions.explanation: --catalog is the Inspector's own editable working set; --config serves someone else's file as-is and guarantees the Inspector will not touch it. They are mutually exclusive and neither combines with an ad-hoc target.

questions.question: In the Inspector CLI, what does exit code 3 mean?

options.text: The tool returned isError: true
The server requires authentication (401/403, WWW-Authenticate, OAuth)
The server was unreachable
No MCP App was found on the tool

questions.question: How do --tool-arg and --tool-args-json differ when passing tool arguments in the Inspector CLI?

options.text: They are identical except for quoting style
--tool-arg coerces values by JSON-parsing them (so "012" becomes 12), while --tool-args-json passes the whole object verbatim with no coercion; the two are mutually exclusive
--tool-args-json only works over HTTP transports
--tool-arg supports at most one argument

questions.explanation: --tool-arg key=value JSON-parses each value (count=1 becomes a number), which can surprise you with strings like "012". --tool-args-json takes the entire argument object at once and passes it verbatim. They cannot be combined.

questions.question: Which CLI flag is recommended for CI runs so the Inspector never starts interactive OAuth and fails fast if no stored token exists?

options.text: --use-stored-auth
--stored-auth-only
--relogin
--wait-for-auth 0

questions.question: Why must the Inspector's OAuth callback URL bind a loopback host (localhost, 127.0.0.0/8, or [::1])?

options.text: Authorization servers only allow loopback redirect URIs
The local callback listener receives the authorization code over plaintext http, so any non-loopback host is rejected — and there is no flag to override this
DNS resolution is disabled in the Inspector
IPv6 is not supported

questions.explanation: Because the code arrives over plaintext http, binding anything but loopback would expose it on the network. The web client listens on http://localhost:6274/oauth/callback and the CLI/TUI share http://127.0.0.1:6276/oauth/callback; if your browser is on another machine, forward the port instead.

questions.question: Which pair of web-backend environment variables should NEVER be combined?

options.text: HOST and CLIENT_PORT
DANGEROUSLY_OMIT_AUTH and DANGEROUSLY_BIND_ALL_INTERFACES
ALLOWED_ORIGINS and NO_PROXY
MCP_DEBUG and DEBUG

questions.question: What does the bare -- separator do in an Inspector web/CLI invocation like mcp-inspector node build/index.js -- --config /etc/myserver.conf?

Everything after -- is passed to the target server command as its own arguments, so flags like --config aren't eaten by the Inspector
It switches the Inspector into verbose mode
It separates multiple servers

questions.question: What is the minimum Node.js version required to run the MCP Inspector?

Node 22.19.0 or newer

Any version with npx

questions.question: SCENARIO: Your CI pipeline must fail the build if the server doesn't expose a tool named get_weather, without any interactive login. Which invocation matches the docs' recipe?

options.text: mcp-inspector --web and a human checks the browser
mcp-inspector --cli --config ./ci-servers.json --server my-server --stored-auth-only --method tools/list --format json | jq -e '.result.tools | map(.name) | index("get_weather")'
curl the server directly with no protocol handshake
mcp-inspector --tui with expect scripts

questions.question: What does the CLI's --app-info flag do?

options.text: Prints the Inspector's version
Reports whether a tool ships an MCP App UI (its ui:// resource, CSP, permissions) WITHOUT calling the tool, so pipelines can decide if a browser is needed
Installs the app locally
Opens the app in the default browser

questions.explanation: --app-info probes tools for MCP App UIs without invoking them. With tools/call it emits one JSON line; with tools/list it emits NDJSON per tool. Exit codes distinguish outcomes: 0 has app, 2 no app, 5 missing tool.

questions.question: SCENARIO: Two CLI OAuth flows run concurrently on one machine and the second fails with EADDRINUSE. Why, and what are the documented workarounds?

options.text: The OAuth state file is corrupted; delete ~/.mcp-inspector

Only one process can hold the default callback port (6276) at a time; use a different fixed port per instance via --callback-url, or http://127.0.0.1:0/... for an OS-assigned ephemeral port if the auth server supports dynamic redirect-URI registration
The server blocked the client's IP
Node 22 removed concurrent sockets

questions.explanation: The CLI and TUI share the loopback callback listener on port 6276, and only one process can bind it. Workarounds: distinct fixed ports per instance, or port 0 for an ephemeral port — remembering redirect URIs must exactly match what's registered.

questions.question: What does the Inspector's 'protocol era' setting control?

options.text: The UI color theme
Whether the connection negotiates legacy MCP (initialize handshake, ≤2025-11-25) or modern MCP (2026-07-28: per-request metadata, server/discover, sessionless), with an auto mode that probes
Whether logs are shown
The OAuth grant type

questions.explanation: All three Inspector clients share protocol-era negotiation: legacy uses the initialize handshake, modern uses per-request _meta and server/discover with sessionless HTTP, and protocolEra can be set to auto, modern, or legacy (defaulting to legacy in catalog files).

questions.question: Which client configs can the Inspector's web client import to populate its catalog?

options.text: Only its own catalog format
Existing configs from Claude Desktop, Cursor, Cline, or VS Code — or a registry server.json
Only Docker Compose files
Kubernetes manifests

questions.question: Where in the Inspector's web client can you review OAuth discovery results, the registered client, granted scopes, and clear OAuth state?

options.text: The Connection Info panel
The browser's address bar
A separate desktop app
Only in the server's logs

questions.explanation: The web client's Connection Info panel shows discovery results, the registered client, granted scopes, and token state, and offers a 'Clear OAuth state' action. The TUI exposes the same fields in its Auth tab (opened with 'a').

questions.question: SCENARIO: Mid-session, a request to a connected server fails with 403 insufficient_scope. What does the Inspector do?

options.text: Drops the connection and requires a full restart

Handles step-up without dropping the connection: it re-authorizes for the union of held and required scopes (banner in web, y/N prompt on stderr in CLI), so the new token covers everything the old one did plus the new scopes
Silently retries with the same token forever
Deletes the stored OAuth state

questions.explanation: Mid-session re-authorization covers both cases: 401 (expired/revoked → re-run flow and retry) and 403 insufficient_scope (step-up for the scope union). Enterprise-managed step-up re-mints silently with no prompt.

questions.question: How does the TUI differ from the web and CLI clients in server selection from a catalog/config file?

The --server flag is web/CLI-only; the TUI loads every server in the file and lets you choose interactively
The TUI only supports HTTP servers
The TUI requires a separate catalog format

questions.question: What is the key difference between the Inspector's --catalog and --config flags?

options.text: --catalog is CLI-only; --config is web-only

--catalog is the Inspector's own writable server list (default ~/.mcp-inspector/mcp.json, created and seeded if missing); --config is read-only, never written or seeded, and errors if the file is missing - and the two are mutually exclusive
--config supports HTTP servers; --catalog supports only stdio
They are aliases for the same behavior

questions.explanation: --catalog = your working set (web-editable, seeded with samples in the web client, empty {} for CLI/TUI). --config = a read-only session against a file you did not write, guaranteed untouched. Passing both is rejected by all three clients. (Inspector docs, Configuration and flags.)

questions.question: An Inspector CLI run in CI exits with code 3. Another exits with code 5. What happened?

options.text: 3 = server unreachable; 5 = usage error
3 = server requires authentication (401/403, OAuth); 5 = tools/call returned isError: true or the tool was not found
3 = no MCP App on the tool; 5 = success with warnings
3 = timeout; 5 = malformed catalog

questions.question: Which flag makes Inspector CLI authentication predictable in CI, and what does it do?

options.text: --relogin: forces a fresh browser OAuth flow
--stored-auth-only: never starts interactive OAuth or step-up and never auto-opens a browser; uses tokens from the shared store if present, otherwise fails immediately with auth_required
--wait-for-auth: blocks for 15 minutes on the callback
--print-handoff: disables auth entirely

questions.question: Why must DANGEROUSLY_OMIT_AUTH never be combined with DANGEROUSLY_BIND_ALL_INTERFACES on the Inspector web backend?

options.text: The flags conflict and crash the process

The backend spawns processes and holds OAuth tokens; removing the session-token check while binding 0.0.0.0 lets anyone who can reach the port drive it - effectively remote code execution plus token theft
It disables the MCP Apps sandbox port
It breaks the ALLOWED_ORIGINS allow-list

questions.explanation: Individually each flag has narrow uses; together they expose an unauthenticated process-spawning, token-holding backend to the network. Relatedly, the OAuth callback URL must stay on loopback (default 127.0.0.1:6276) because the code arrives over plaintext http; the web UI defaults to port 6274. (Inspector docs, Configuration and flags.)

questions.question: Where does Claude Desktop write its MCP-related log files on macOS?

Send everything via notifications/message, the recommended mechanism
HTTP servers cannot log at all

questions.question: A request is rejected with error code -32021 (MissingRequiredClientCapabilityError). What does this indicate?

options.text: The server does not support the requested protocol version
The server needs a capability (such as elicitation) that the request's clientCapabilities in _meta did not declare
The tool arguments failed schema validation
The OAuth token expired

By contrast, -32022 (UnsupportedProtocolVersionError) lists the server's supported versions, and -32602 (Invalid params) covers requests missing required _meta fields or otherwise malformed input.

questions.question: MCP servers launched over stdio inherit only a limited set of environment variables. How do you provide additional ones in claude_desktop_config.json?

Use a .envrc file next to the config

questions.question: How do clients opt in to receiving log messages from a server under the 2026-07-28 per-request logging model?

By setting the io.modelcontextprotocol/logLevel field in the request's _meta; servers must not send notifications/message for requests that omit it
Logging is always on at debug level
By subscribing to a logs:// resource

questions.question: How do you enable Chrome DevTools inside Claude Desktop for client-side debugging?

Install a separate debug build of Claude

questions.question: For a local stdio server, what happens to messages the server writes to stderr?

They are captured automatically by the host application (e.g., into Claude Desktop's mcp-server-NAME.log)
They corrupt the protocol like stdout does
They are sent to the model as context

Only fatal crashes
User passwords for reproduction
Nothing; logging slows servers down

The Windows Event Viewer only

questions.question: How many log severity levels does MCP define, and from which standard do they come?

Eight levels (debug through emergency) from RFC 5424 (syslog)

Ten custom levels

questions.question: SCENARIO: Your server runs perfectly when you launch it from your project directory in a terminal, but fails to find its data files when Claude Desktop launches it. What's the most likely cause?

The server uses relative paths, and the working directory of a client-launched server may be undefined (like / on macOS) — switch to absolute paths in config and .env files
The transport changed from stdio to HTTP
Node and Python resolve paths differently

questions.question: SCENARIO: A hand-rolled client's requests are all rejected with error -32602 (Invalid params), even simple tools/list calls. Given the 2026-07-28 per-request metadata rules, what should you check first?

Whether the JSON-RPC id is a UUID
Whether OAuth scopes include mcp:tools

Call server/discover to see the server's supported versions; if you get UnsupportedProtocolVersionError (-32022), its data field lists the versions the server supports, so you can pick a mutual one

The MCP Inspector — while configuration or server-code changes in a client like Claude Desktop require a full client restart
Editing the model's system prompt
tcpdump
