questions.question: How is JSON-RPC described in the opening of its specification?

options.text: A stateless, light-weight remote procedure call (RPC) protocol that is transport agnostic
A stateful streaming protocol tied to HTTP/2
A binary serialization format
A database query language

questions.explanation: JSON-RPC is a stateless, light-weight RPC protocol using JSON as its data format. It is transport agnostic — usable in-process, over sockets, over HTTP, or in other message-passing environments — which is why MCP can run it over both stdio and Streamable HTTP.

questions.question: What value must the jsonrpc member of every request and response contain?

options.text: Exactly the String "2.0"
The number 2
Any version string the server prefers
It is optional

questions.explanation: The jsonrpc member MUST be exactly "2.0". This is also how 2.0 messages are distinguished from JSON-RPC 1.0, which lacks the member.

questions.question: Which members can a JSON-RPC 2.0 Request object contain?

options.text: jsonrpc, method, params (optional), and id
url, headers, and body
type, payload, and checksum
jsonrpc, function, and args

questions.explanation: A request carries jsonrpc ("2.0"), method (a String naming the method), optional params (a Structured value), and id (String, Number, or Null) — omit the id and the request becomes a notification.

questions.question: What is a JSON-RPC Notification?

options.text: A response the server sends without being asked
A Request object without an id member — the client isn't interested in a response, and the server MUST NOT reply
Any message with id: 0
A batch of exactly one request

questions.explanation: A notification is a request with no id. No response is returned — even for errors — so notifications are not confirmable. MCP uses this for messages like notifications/tools/list_changed.

questions.question: What are the two allowed parameter structures for params?

options.text: By-position (an Array in the server's expected order) or by-name (an Object with exactly-matching, case-sensitive member names)
Comma-separated strings or XML
Only flat key=value pairs
Positional integers only

questions.explanation: If present, params MUST be Structured: an Array for by-position calls, or an Object for by-name calls whose names must match the method's expected parameters exactly, including case. MCP uses by-name params.

questions.question: Which rule governs the result and error members of a Response object?

options.text: Both must always be present
Exactly one must be included: result is required on success, error on failure, and both MUST NOT appear together
result may contain an error object
error is optional even on failure

questions.explanation: A response contains either result (success) or error (failure), never both. The response also echoes the request's id so the client can correlate them.

questions.question: What are the members of a JSON-RPC Error object?

options.text: code (an integer), message (a concise String), and optional data with additional information
status, reason, and stacktrace
errno and strerror
level, source, and detail

questions.explanation: The error object has code (MUST be an integer), message (a short single-sentence description), and optional data (Primitive or Structured, server-defined). MCP uses data e.g. to list supported versions in an UnsupportedProtocolVersionError.

questions.question: Match the reserved error code to its meaning: -32700, -32600, -32601, -32602, -32603.

options.text: Parse error, Invalid Request, Method not found, Invalid params, Internal error
Internal error, Parse error, Invalid params, Method not found, Invalid Request
Timeout, Overload, Not found, Bad gateway, Unavailable
They are all synonyms for 'server error'

questions.explanation: -32700 Parse error (invalid JSON), -32600 Invalid Request, -32601 Method not found, -32602 Invalid params, -32603 Internal error. -32000 to -32099 are reserved for implementation-defined server errors, and the whole -32768..-32000 range is reserved.

questions.question: Which range of error codes is reserved for implementation-defined server errors?
questions.explanation: -32000 to -32099 is reserved for implementation-defined server errors within the larger reserved range -32768 to -32000. MCP defines codes such as -32021 and -32022 for protocol-specific failures. The remainder of the space is available for application-defined errors.

questions.question: What restrictions and recommendations apply to the id member of a Request?

options.text: It must be a UUID
It MUST be a String, Number, or Null if included; Null is discouraged (it's used for responses with unknown id), and Numbers SHOULD NOT contain fractional parts
It must increase monotonically
Booleans are allowed

questions.explanation: The id is client-established and echoed back by the server. Null is discouraged because error responses to unparseable requests use id: null, and fractional numbers are discouraged since many decimal fractions can't be represented exactly in binary.

questions.question: SCENARIO: A server receives {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "foobar", "id": "1"} but has no method named foobar. What does it return?

options.text: {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "error": {"code": -32601, "message": "Method not found"}, "id": "1"}
An empty 200 response
{"result": null, "id": "1"}
Nothing; unknown methods are ignored

questions.explanation: A call to a non-existent method returns error -32601 Method not found, echoing the request's id — this example appears verbatim in the specification.

questions.question: SCENARIO: A server receives text that is not valid JSON at all. What id does the error response carry, and why?

options.text: The id from the broken request, recovered heuristically
id: null — because the id could not be detected in the malformed request, the spec mandates Null (with error -32700 Parse error)
A freshly generated id
No response is ever sent for parse errors

questions.explanation: When there is an error detecting the id (Parse error / Invalid Request), the response id MUST be Null. This is also why using Null as a request id is discouraged — it's reserved for 'unknown id' responses.

questions.question: Which statements about batch calls are correct?

options.text: Responses must be returned in the same order as the requests

The server may process batch requests concurrently and return responses in any order; clients match them by id. Notifications in a batch get no response, and a batch of all notifications returns nothing at all
Batches may contain at most 10 requests
An empty array [] is a valid no-op batch

questions.explanation: Batch responses MAY come back in any order (match by id), notifications get no response objects, and if no responses remain the server returns nothing rather than an empty array. An empty array is invalid and yields a single -32600 error.

questions.question: Which method names are reserved in JSON-RPC 2.0?

options.text: Names beginning with 'rpc.' (rpc followed by a period) — reserved for rpc-internal methods and extensions
Names containing underscores
Names longer than 32 characters
Names beginning with capital letters

questions.explanation: Method names beginning with rpc. are reserved for system extensions and MUST NOT be used for anything else. MCP's method names (tools/list, server/discover, etc.) use slash-separated namespaces, avoiding the reserved prefix.

questions.question: SCENARIO: In an MCP session you observe the message {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "notifications/tools/list_changed", "params": {...}} with no id field, and the client sends nothing back. Is this correct JSON-RPC behavior?

options.text: No; every message requires a response
Yes: a request without an id is a notification, and per JSON-RPC 2.0 the receiver MUST NOT reply — exactly how MCP delivers change notifications
No; the server should have used id: null
Only if the transport is HTTP

questions.explanation: This ties MCP back to its JSON-RPC foundation: notifications omit the id, expect no response, and receivers must not reply. MCP's notifications/* messages follow these semantics precisely.

questions.question: Match the MCP-specific error codes introduced in 2026-07-28: -32020, -32021, -32022.

options.text: HeaderMismatch, MissingRequiredClientCapability, UnsupportedProtocolVersion
UnsupportedProtocolVersion, HeaderMismatch, MissingRequiredClientCapability
MissingRequiredClientCapability, UnsupportedProtocolVersion, HeaderMismatch
ParseError, InvalidRequest, MethodNotFound

questions.explanation: Memory hook: '20-21-22 = Header, Capability, Version'. -32020 HeaderMismatch, -32021 MissingRequiredClientCapability, -32022 UnsupportedProtocolVersion. (Spec basic/index, error codes.)

questions.question: How does 2026-07-28 partition the JSON-RPC implementation-defined server-error range (-32000 to -32099)?

options.text: The whole range is now reserved for the MCP specification
-32000 to -32019 is legacy implementation territory (grandfathered; no NEW codes may be allocated there), while -32020 to -32099 is reserved exclusively for the MCP specification
-32000 to -32049 for clients, -32050 to -32099 for servers
The range is deprecated; all errors must use positive codes

questions.explanation: New codes MUST NOT be allocated in -32000..-32019, and implementations MUST NOT emit undefined codes from the spec-reserved -32020..-32099 sub-range. Codes for new purposes SHOULD live outside the JSON-RPC reserved range entirely. (Spec basic/index, error code allocation policy.)

questions.question: A modern client requests a nonexistent resource URI. Which error should the server emit, and how should the client treat -32002?

options.text: Emit -32002; clients must reject -32602
Emit -32602 (Invalid params); the server MUST NOT emit -32002, but clients SHOULD still accept -32002 from servers on earlier protocol versions
Emit -32601 (Method not found)
Emit HTTP 404 with no JSON-RPC body

questions.explanation: SEP-2164 moved resource-not-found from -32002 to -32602 to align with JSON-RPC. -32002 (and -32042) remain reserved-but-forbidden for modern servers, while clients keep accepting them for backward compatibility. Trap 10 material. (Spec basic/index and changelog.)

questions.question: Which statement about JSON-RPC request IDs is specific to MCP and stricter than base JSON-RPC 2.0?

options.text: IDs may be floats
The ID MUST NOT be null, MUST be a string or integer, and MUST NOT match any other request the sender has issued and not yet received a response for
IDs must be UUIDv4 strings
IDs are optional on requests

questions.explanation: Base JSON-RPC merely discourages null IDs; MCP forbids them outright and requires uniqueness among the sender's outstanding requests. Notifications still carry no ID at all. (Spec basic/index, Requests.)

questions.question: A client sends a request pinned to protocol version 2025-11-25 to a server that only supports 2026-07-28. What does the modern spec say happens?

options.text: The server silently answers in its own version
The server returns UnsupportedProtocolVersionError (-32022); the client could have avoided this by checking supportedVersions via server/discover first
The server downgrades and emulates the legacy handshake
The transport layer rejects the TCP connection

questions.explanation: Version mismatches surface as UnsupportedProtocolVersionError. Negotiation detects mismatch - it does not bridge eras; a dual-era server routes per request, but a modern-only server errors. (Spec 2026-07-28 changelog, major change 2; server/discover.)

questions.question: How are JSON-RPC messages exchanged over the stdio transport?

options.text: The client launches the server as a subprocess; messages flow over the server's standard input and output, and stderr is reserved for logging
Over a Unix socket created by the server
Via shared memory segments
Through temporary files polled every second

questions.explanation: With stdio, the host launches the server process and speaks JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout — which is why any stray stdout output (print, console.log) corrupts the protocol, and logging must go to stderr.

questions.question: How does the Streamable HTTP transport exchange messages?

options.text: WebSocket frames only
HTTP POST for client-to-server messages, with optional Server-Sent Events for streaming server output
gRPC bidirectional streams
FTP file transfers

questions.explanation: Streamable HTTP uses HTTP POST for client-to-server messages with optional SSE for streaming. It enables remote servers and supports standard HTTP authentication (bearer tokens, API keys, custom headers), with OAuth recommended for obtaining tokens.

questions.question: Which HTTP header is now required on EVERY Streamable HTTP POST request in 2026-07-28?

options.text: Mcp-Session-Id
Mcp-Method (with Mcp-Name additionally required for tools/call, resources/read, and prompts/get)
X-Requested-With
Mcp-Token

questions.explanation: SEP-2243 requires the Mcp-Method header on every request; Mcp-Name is required for the request types that name a target (tools/call, resources/read, prompts/get). Gateways, rate limiters, and WAFs can then route and meter on headers without parsing the JSON body.

questions.question: SCENARIO: A Streamable HTTP request arrives with the header Mcp-Name: search but the JSON body actually calls the tool 'delete_records'. What must a server that processes the body do?

options.text: Trust the body silently
Reject the request — headers and body that disagree yield 400 Bad Request with the HeaderMismatch JSON-RPC error (-32020)
Execute both tools
Trust the header and call 'search'

questions.explanation: Because intermediaries may authorize on headers, the spec anticipates spoofing: servers reject requests where the headers and body disagree, returning 400 with the HeaderMismatchError (-32020, renumbered from -32001).

questions.question: What happened to the Mcp-Session-Id header in the 2026-07-28 revision?

options.text: It was made mandatory
It was removed along with protocol-level sessions — list endpoints no longer vary per connection, and cross-call state uses explicit server-minted handles passed as tool arguments
It was renamed to Mcp-Connection-Id
It now carries the OAuth token

questions.explanation: SEP-2567 removed sessions and Mcp-Session-Id. This eliminates sticky routing and shared session stores, letting servers run behind ordinary round-robin load balancers and on serverless platforms.

questions.question: SCENARIO: An SSE response stream breaks mid-request under 2026-07-28. Your legacy code tries to resume with the Last-Event-ID header. What actually happens?

options.text: The server replays missed events from the event ID
Resumability and message redelivery were removed: a broken response stream loses the in-flight request, and the client MUST re-issue it as a new request with a new request ID
The server pauses the request until reconnection
The stream automatically migrates to WebSocket

questions.explanation: SEP-2575 removed SSE stream resumability (Last-Event-ID and SSE event IDs). Losing the stream loses the in-flight request; the client re-issues it fresh with a new request ID.

questions.question: What is the x-mcp-header annotation used for?

options.text: Marking a header as deprecated
Letting a tool parameter be mirrored into a custom HTTP header (e.g., a 'city' argument annotated x-mcp-header: "City" appears as Mcp-Param-City), so infrastructure can route on parameter values
Encrypting individual headers
Declaring the server's version

questions.explanation: SEP-2243 adds support for custom headers derived from tool parameters via x-mcp-header schema annotations, surfacing selected argument values as Mcp-Param-* headers for gateways.

questions.question: How does progress reporting work for a long-running MCP request?

options.text: The client polls a /progress REST endpoint
The client includes a progressToken in the request's _meta; the server emits notifications/progress carrying that token, and the client matches notifications back to the originating call
Progress is emailed to the user
Progress is only available via the Tasks extension

questions.explanation: progressToken is a reserved _meta key (part of RequestMetaObject in the 2026-07-28 schema). Servers send notifications/progress tagged with the token; these request-scoped notifications flow on the response stream of the request they relate to, not the subscriptions/listen stream.

questions.question: On which stream do request-scoped notifications such as notifications/progress travel in 2026-07-28?

options.text: The subscriptions/listen stream, like all notifications
The response stream of the request they relate to
A dedicated WebSocket
They are batched into the final result

questions.explanation: The changelog is explicit: request-scoped notifications like notifications/progress and notifications/message continue to flow on the response stream of their originating request; subscriptions/listen carries only the opted-in change notifications.

questions.question: How does pagination work for list operations like tools/list?

options.text: Clients pass page and pageSize integers
Cursor-based: the client passes an opaque cursor token representing the current position, and the server returns results starting after it (with a next cursor when more remain)
Servers always return everything in one response
Pagination uses HTTP Range headers

questions.explanation: The schema defines Cursor as 'an opaque token representing the current pagination position'; list requests accept an optional cursor parameter, and clients treat it as opaque rather than parsing or constructing it.

questions.question: Which server utility helps users fill in valid values for prompt arguments and resource template parameters?

options.text: Completion (argument autocompletion, e.g., suggesting 'Paris' for a partial 'Par')
Sampling
Caching
Progress

questions.explanation: The completion utility provides autocompletion for prompt arguments and resource template parameters, letting users discover valid values without knowing exact formats.

questions.question: SCENARIO: A tools/list response arrives with ttlMs: 300000 and cacheScope: "public". Then a notifications/tools/list_changed arrives after two minutes. Can the client keep using its cached list for the remaining three minutes?

options.text: Yes; the TTL always wins
No — a cached list must be treated as stale once a list_changed notification arrives, even before its TTL expires
Only if cacheScope is private
Yes, but only for read operations

questions.explanation: ttlMs is a freshness hint and cacheScope (public/private) governs shared-intermediary caching, but the caching rules say a list_changed notification supersedes the TTL: treat the cached list as stale immediately.

questions.question: Why does the 2026-07-28 spec recommend servers return tools from tools/list in a deterministic order?

options.text: Alphabetical order is easier to read
A stable order enables client-side caching and improves LLM prompt cache hit rates, since the tools array often sits in the cached prompt prefix
JSON requires sorted arrays
It prevents pagination

questions.explanation: This minor change recognizes that tool definitions live in the model's prompt: if their order shifts between calls, prompt caches are invalidated. Deterministic ordering keeps both client caches and provider prompt caches effective.

questions.question: SCENARIO: Your ops team wants per-tool rate limiting at the API gateway without decrypting and parsing JSON-RPC bodies. Which 2026-07-28 feature makes this practical?

options.text: Sticky sessions keyed on Mcp-Session-Id
The required Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name headers: the invoked method and target tool are visible in HTTP headers, so gateways, WAFs, and rate limiters can route, meter, and authorize at the edge
Base64-encoding the request body
Switching to the stdio transport

questions.explanation: Header-based routing (SEP-2243) is designed exactly for this: a tools/call to 'search' arrives as Mcp-Method: tools/call and Mcp-Name: search, making per-tool policy at the edge practical without body inspection.

questions.question: How does a client cancel an in-flight request?

options.text: By closing the TCP connection, which servers interpret as cancellation
By sending a notifications/cancelled notification referencing the requestId; the server should stop work and free resources, sending no response for the cancelled request
By calling DELETE /requests/{id}
Requests cannot be cancelled in MCP

questions.explanation: Cancellation is one of MCP's cross-cutting patterns: a JSON-RPC notification (notifications/cancelled) carries the requestId of the in-flight request; being a notification, it expects no reply, and the cancelled request produces no response.

questions.question: Under SEP-2243, which Streamable HTTP POST messages must carry the Mcp-Method header, and why does it exist?

options.text: Only tools/call; it enables retries
All requests AND notifications; it lets load balancers, gateways, and WAFs route and apply policy without parsing (or even decrypting) the JSON body
Only requests with an id; notifications are exempt
Only requests to legacy servers

questions.explanation: Mcp-Method mirrors the JSON-RPC method for every POST, including notifications, so intermediaries avoid deep packet inspection. Mcp-Name additionally accompanies tools/call, resources/read, and prompts/get. (SEP-2243, Standard Headers.)

questions.question: What value does the Mcp-Name header carry for each of tools/call, resources/read, and prompts/get?

options.text: params.name for tools/call and prompts/get, and params.uri for resources/read
params.uri for all three
The server's registry name
The JSON-RPC id

questions.explanation: Mcp-Name mirrors the target's identifier: the tool name, the resource URI, or the prompt name. It is required on exactly those three request types. (SEP-2243, Standard Headers table.)

questions.question: A gateway routes on Mcp-Name: tenant-a while the body actually calls a tool for tenant-b. How must a body-processing server respond, and what attack does this rule block?

options.text: Honor the body silently - headers are advisory

Reject with HTTP 400 and JSON-RPC HeaderMismatch (-32020 in the final spec; originally numbered -32001 in the SEP), preventing header spoofing that routes around security policy while executing a different operation
Return 403 insufficient_scope
Strip the header and forward downstream

questions.explanation: Any component that processes the body MUST validate headers against body values and reject mismatches with 400 + HeaderMismatch. Otherwise a malicious client could evade region routing, tenant rate limits, or WAF policy. Note the renumbering: -32001 -> -32020. (SEP-2243 server behavior + changelog minor change 12.)

questions.question: Which x-mcp-header rule set is correct for custom Mcp-Param-* headers?

options.text: Any JSON type may be mirrored, including objects

Only primitive types (string, integer, boolean - explicitly NOT number); values must be case-insensitively unique in the schema; clients MUST reject violating tool definitions by excluding that tool from tools/list; sensitive parameters SHOULD NOT be marked since headers are visible to intermediaries
Only top-level required parameters may be mirrored
The feature is optional for clients but mandatory for servers

questions.explanation: x-mcp-header is limited to primitives (number is excluded; integers within the JS safe range), names must be unique case-insensitively and match HTTP token syntax, invalid definitions cause the client to drop that one tool (not the whole list), and passwords/API keys/PII should never be mirrored. Servers MAY use the feature; clients MUST support it. (SEP-2243, custom headers.)

questions.question: A tool argument value is "Hello, 世界". How does the client transmit it in an Mcp-Param-* header?

options.text: As-is - HTTP headers accept UTF-8
Base64-encoded with the sentinel wrapper, e.g. Mcp-Param-Greeting: =?base64?...?=, because non-ASCII values (like leading/trailing whitespace or control characters) cannot ride as plain header values
URL-encoded with %XX escapes
The header is silently omitted

questions.explanation: Values with non-ASCII characters, leading/trailing whitespace, or control characters MUST be Base64-encoded and wrapped in the case-sensitive =?base64?...?= sentinel. Plain ASCII values like us-west1 travel readably. Header names are case-insensitive; method values are case-sensitive. (SEP-2243, Value Encoding.)

questions.question: What are MCP extensions?

options.text: Mandatory add-ons every implementation must support
Optional, versioned additions to the core protocol that require explicit support from both client and server, negotiated via the extension capabilities mechanism
Browser plugins for the Inspector
Paid features licensed by Anthropic

questions.explanation: Extensions add modular, specialized, or experimental functionality beyond the core protocol. They are always opt-in and negotiated: clients declare them in the extensions field of clientCapabilities, and servers advertise theirs via server/discover.

questions.question: What format do extension identifiers follow?

options.text: {vendor-prefix}/{extension-name}, e.g., io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks; official extensions use the io.modelcontextprotocol prefix
Sequential integers assigned by the registry
UUIDs
ext-<name>-v<number> only

questions.explanation: Extensions are identified as {vendor-prefix}/{extension-name}. Official extensions use the io.modelcontextprotocol vendor prefix and live in MCP GitHub org repositories with an ext- prefix (ext-apps, ext-tasks, ext-auth).

questions.question: How is extension support negotiated in the 2026-07-28 protocol?

options.text: Via a dedicated extensions/negotiate RPC

Clients declare supported extensions in the extensions field of the io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities sent in each request's _meta; servers advertise theirs in the capabilities returned by server/discover
By exchanging config files out of band
Extensions are enabled by default unless disabled

questions.explanation: The changelog added an extensions field to both ClientCapabilities and ServerCapabilities. Both sides must declare support — extensions are never active by default.

questions.question: What do MCP Apps enable?

options.text: Running MCP servers inside mobile apps
Servers delivering interactive UI elements (charts, forms, dashboards, video players) that render inline within conversations in MCP hosts
Compiling servers to native binaries
App-store distribution of servers

questions.explanation: MCP Apps let tools return interactive HTML interfaces rendered directly in the chat — data visualizations, forms, dashboards — instead of only text and structured data.

questions.question: How does an MCP App link a tool to its user interface?

options.text: The tool declares a UI resource using the ui:// URI scheme, and references it via metadata (_meta.ui.resourceUri) so the host can fetch and render it
The tool returns raw HTML in its text content
The host guesses the UI from the tool name
UIs are uploaded to the registry separately

questions.explanation: MCP Apps introduces predeclared UI resources on the ui:// scheme (MIME type text/html;profile=mcp-app), tool-UI linkage via _meta.ui.resourceUri, and bidirectional communication — the extension identifier is io.modelcontextprotocol/ui.

questions.question: SCENARIO: A user clicks a button inside an MCP App's rendered widget, which triggers another tool call. From a security standpoint, how does this action flow?

options.text: The iframe calls the server's API directly over the network

The UI runs in a mandatory sandboxed iframe and communicates with the host via JSON-RPC over postMessage; the tool call is proxied through the host and goes through the host's ordinary audit and consent path
The click is converted to a shell command
UI actions bypass consent because the user already approved rendering

questions.explanation: MCP Apps' security model: mandatory iframe sandboxing, host-constructed CSP from server-declared domains (default deny-all network), and auditable JSON-RPC/postMessage communication. A UI-triggered tool call gets the same consent treatment as a direct one.

questions.question: What problem does the Tasks extension solve?

options.text: Slow JSON parsing
Long-running operations: instead of blocking, the server returns a durable task handle so clients can poll for progress, provide mid-flight input, and retrieve the result even after reconnecting
Scheduling cron jobs on the client
Compressing large tool results

questions.explanation: Tasks (io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks) address CI pipelines, batch processing, human approvals, and similar work: no long-lived connections, crash resilience via durable task IDs, progress visibility, and mid-flight interaction.

questions.question: How is a task returned to the client, and how does the client get the result?

options.text: Via a webhook the client registers

The server returns a CreateTaskResult (resultType: "task") with a taskId, initial status, TTL, and suggested poll interval; the client polls tasks/get (respecting pollIntervalMs) until a terminal status, where result or error appears
The server emails the result
The client blocks on tasks/result

questions.explanation: The 2026-07-28 redesign replaced the blocking tasks/result with polling via tasks/get (plus tasks/update for input and tasks/cancel). The task must be durably created before the CreateTaskResult is sent.

questions.question: Which task statuses exist, and which are terminal?

options.text: working, input_required, completed, failed, cancelled — with completed, failed, and cancelled terminal
queued, running, done
open and closed
pending, active, archived, purged

questions.explanation: Tasks carry status metadata: working, input_required (server needs client input via inputRequests/tasks/update), and the terminal states completed (result field), failed (error field), and cancelled. Terminal state never changes.

questions.question: SCENARIO: A server wants to return a task handle for a slow tools/call, but the incoming request's clientCapabilities did not include the tasks extension. What must the server do?

options.text: Return the task anyway; clients must handle it
Never return a task to a client that didn't declare support — verify the extension in the per-request capabilities first, and otherwise process the request synchronously
Return an empty result
Convert the task to an elicitation

questions.explanation: Task creation is server-directed but capability-gated: before returning a CreateTaskResult, the server must verify the client included io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks in its per-request capabilities.

questions.question: Is task cancellation guaranteed to stop the work?

options.text: Yes; tasks/cancel kills the worker immediately
No — cancellation is cooperative: the server acknowledges the intent, but the task may still reach a non-cancelled terminal status
Only if the task is younger than its TTL
Cancellation is not part of the extension

questions.explanation: tasks/cancel signals intent; the server acks with an empty result and honors it when possible, but is not obligated to stop the work.

questions.question: What does the OAuth Client Credentials auth extension add to MCP?

options.text: Passwordless logins for humans
Machine-to-machine authentication via the OAuth 2.1 client credentials flow — no user interaction, using pre-registered client credentials established out of band
Biometric authentication
Anonymous access mode

questions.explanation: io.modelcontextprotocol/oauth-client-credentials enables M2M auth for HTTP-based transports where no user is in the loop (e.g., service-to-service agents), building on the baseline authorization requirements.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) extension?

options.text: Charging enterprises per token

Centralized access control through the organization's identity provider: employees get connected MCP servers on first login with a single sign-on, no per-app OAuth, and the IdP can enforce which users/groups may use which clients with which servers and scopes
Replacing OAuth with API keys
Encrypting all traffic with enterprise certificates

questions.explanation: EMA (now stable) addresses repeated consent prompts in enterprises: the trusted IdP centrally provisions MCP server access — e.g., engineering gets read-only source-control access from a code editor while marketing gets docs read/write — for zero-touch setup.

questions.question: SCENARIO: A monitoring agent (no human user) must call a protected MCP server nightly, while your employees access the same server through the company IdP with zero-touch setup. Which extensions map to each need?

options.text: MCP Apps for the agent; Tasks for the employees
OAuth Client Credentials for the machine-to-machine agent; Enterprise-Managed Authorization for centralized, IdP-driven employee access
Both need Dynamic Client Registration only
Neither; core MCP forbids unattended access

questions.explanation: The two auth extensions cover exactly these cases: client credentials for M2M auth without a user, and EMA for centrally managed employee access through the enterprise IdP. Both require explicit client support and are never active by default.

questions.question: Where do official MCP extensions live, and how can you check which clients support them?

options.text: In npm only; support is universal
In MCP GitHub org repositories prefixed ext- (ext-apps, ext-tasks, ext-auth); the docs publish an extension support matrix showing which MCP clients implement which official extensions
In a private Anthropic repository
Inside the core schema.ts

questions.explanation: Official extensions are developed in ext-* repos under github.com/modelcontextprotocol, and the Extension Support Matrix page (extensions/client-matrix) tracks per-client support — important because support varies and requires explicit opt-in.

questions.question: How is the Tasks extension negotiated in the modern protocol?

options.text: It is on by default for tools/call

The client includes io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks under extensions in its per-request clientCapabilities; the server advertises the same extension in its server/discover capabilities - and a server must never return a task to a client that did not declare support
The server sends notifications/tasks/offer once per connection
The host enables it in claude_desktop_config.json

questions.explanation: Extensions are opt-in on both sides. The server decides per-request whether to create a task (no per-request client flag needed), but only for clients that declared the extension capability. (Tasks extension overview.)

questions.question: Which task methods exist in the redesigned io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks extension, and which were removed?

options.text: tasks/get, tasks/update, tasks/cancel exist; tasks/list was removed and the blocking tasks/result was replaced by polling tasks/get
tasks/list, tasks/get, tasks/result exist; tasks/cancel was removed
Only tasks/get exists
tasks/get, tasks/result, tasks/update exist; tasks/cancel was removed

questions.explanation: The 2026-07-28 redesign removed tasks/list, replaced blocking tasks/result with tasks/get polling, and added tasks/update for client-to-server input. Trap 8: tasks/list and tasks/result do NOT exist. (Changelog major change 6; Tasks extension.)

questions.question: Which task statuses are terminal?

options.text: working and input_required
completed, failed, and cancelled
completed only
cancelled and input_required

questions.explanation: Once a task reaches completed, failed, or cancelled its state never changes. working and input_required are transient. Cancellation is cooperative, so a cancelled request may still finish in another terminal state. (Tasks extension, task lifecycle.)

questions.question: A polled task reports status input_required. How does the client supply the requested information?

options.text: It retries the original tools/call with inputResponses, exactly like core MRTR
It reads the inputRequests map from the tasks/get response and submits the answers via tasks/update (the server acks and ignores unknown or already-satisfied keys)
It opens a second connection for a server-initiated elicitation
It cancels and recreates the task with the answers inline

questions.explanation: Tasks handle mid-flight input through tasks/update rather than retrying the original request - the durable taskId already anchors the state. Servers can also push full task state via notifications/tasks over subscriptions/listen, replacing polls. (Tasks extension, implementation guide.)

questions.question: What is the MCP Registry?

options.text: A package host that stores server code and binaries
The official centralized metadata repository for publicly accessible MCP servers, with namespace management and a REST API for discovery
A paid marketplace run by Anthropic
A DNS service for MCP domains

questions.explanation: The Registry (registry.modelcontextprotocol.io, currently in preview) hosts standardized server metadata — not code. Packages themselves live on npm, PyPI, Docker Hub, etc.; the registry maps server names to those locations.

questions.question: In what file format is a server's registry metadata described?

options.text: server.json — containing the unique name, package/remote location, execution instructions, and discovery data
registry.yaml
mcp.toml
manifest.xml

questions.explanation: server.json is the standardized format: it carries the reverse-DNS server name (e.g., io.github.user/server-name), where to find the server (npm identifier, remote URL), execution details (args, env vars), and description/discovery data.

questions.question: What naming format do registry server names follow, and why?

options.text: Free-form strings chosen by the publisher
Reverse-DNS namespaces (io.github.username/server or com.example/server) tied to verified GitHub accounts or domains, so only the legitimate owner can publish under a namespace
UUIDs generated at publish time
Sequential numeric IDs

questions.explanation: Namespace authentication is the registry's core trust mechanism: io.github.* namespaces are verified via GitHub OAuth, and custom domains (com.example/*) via DNS or HTTP challenges.

questions.question: Which command-line tool publishes servers to the official registry, and what are the key steps?

options.text: npm publish --mcp
mcp-publisher: run init to generate a server.json template, login (e.g., 'mcp-publisher login github'), then publish
git push registry main
docker push registry.modelcontextprotocol.io

questions.explanation: The mcp-publisher CLI drives publishing: init scaffolds server.json with auto-detected values, login authenticates (GitHub OAuth for io.github.* namespaces), and publish submits — with --dry-run available for validation.

questions.question: How does the registry verify you own the npm package referenced in your server.json?

options.text: It doesn't; npm packages are trusted implicitly
It checks that the package.json contains an mcpName property exactly matching the server name from server.json
It requires a signed tarball
It emails the npm maintainer

questions.explanation: Each package type has an ownership-verification marker: npm uses mcpName in package.json; PyPI and NuGet use an 'mcp-name: <server-name>' string in the README (which may be hidden in an HTML comment); all must match the server.json name.

questions.question: How is ownership verified for Docker/OCI images published to the registry?

options.text: Via an io.modelcontextprotocol.server.name annotation/LABEL on the image that must match the server.json name
By scanning the image for a LICENSE file
Docker images cannot be registered
By checking the image digest against npm

questions.explanation: OCI packages (registryType: "oci", supporting Docker Hub, ghcr.io, *.pkg.dev, *.azurecr.io, mcr.microsoft.com) are verified via the io.modelcontextprotocol.server.name annotation, e.g., a Dockerfile LABEL matching the server name.

questions.question: SCENARIO: You publish an MCPB package to the registry. Which two verification requirements apply to the artifact and its metadata?

options.text: The file must be under 10 MB and GPG-signed
The artifact URL (identifier) must contain the string 'mcp', and server.json must include a fileSha256 hash — which MCP clients (not the registry) validate before installation
It must be hosted on npm
MCPB packages need no verification

questions.explanation: MCPB packages must be hosted via GitHub or GitLab releases, the identifier URL must contain 'mcp' (e.g., via the .mcpb extension), and fileSha256 is required. The registry itself doesn't validate the hash; clients validate it for file integrity.

questions.question: SCENARIO: mcp-publisher fails with 'You do not have permission to publish this server' after GitHub login. What's the most likely mismatch?

options.text: Your npm token expired
Your authentication method doesn't match the namespace: with GitHub auth, the server name must start with io.github.<your-username>/
server.json is missing a description
The registry is read-only on weekends

questions.explanation: This documented error means the auth method and namespace format disagree — GitHub-authenticated publishers can only publish under io.github.<username>/ (or their org); custom com.example/* namespaces need DNS/HTTP verification instead.

questions.question: Can you publish a remote (hosted) MCP server to the registry without any installable package?

options.text: No; a package is always required

Yes — server.json supports a remotes field (with transport type and URL), which can also coexist with packages; for com.yourcompany/* namespaces, remote URLs must be on that company's domain or subdomains
Only for SSE transports
Only after a manual review

questions.explanation: Remote servers are first-class: the remotes array lists transport type and URL (plus optional required headers). Domain-namespace publishers face URL restrictions binding remotes to their verified domain; io.github.* namespaces have no URL restriction.

questions.question: Does the official MCP Registry support private servers?

options.text: Yes, with a paid plan
No — it's designed for publicly accessible servers; for private servers (private networks or private package registries) the recommendation is to host your own private MCP registry
Yes, if they use OAuth
Only for enterprise customers

questions.explanation: The registry supports open- and closed-source servers as long as the installation method or the server itself is publicly accessible. Private servers (e.g., mcp.acme-corp.internal) belong in a self-hosted private registry implementing the same OpenAPI spec.

questions.question: Who is the primary intended consumer of the official MCP Registry's API?

options.text: End users browsing manually

Downstream aggregators (e.g., MCP marketplaces), which pull metadata on a regular but infrequent basis and add curation or ratings; host applications should consume those sub-registries rather than the official registry directly
LLMs at inference time
Package registries like npm

questions.explanation: The registry's metadata is deliberately unopinionated. Aggregators consume it (roughly hourly), layer curation on top, and expose the same OpenAPI interface; host applications are meant to consume aggregators, not the official registry directly.

questions.question: How does the official registry handle security scanning of server code?

options.text: It runs a full sandbox analysis of every package
It delegates scanning to the underlying package registries (npm, PyPI, Docker Hub) and to downstream aggregators, focusing itself on namespace authentication and metadata hosting
Publishers self-certify with a checkbox
All code is manually audited by maintainers

questions.explanation: The registry's trust model: namespace auth proves the publisher's identity; actual code scanning is delegated to package registries' own security tooling and to aggregators/marketplaces that can add checks, ratings, or curation.

questions.question: Which mechanisms does the registry use to prevent spam?

options.text: Namespace authentication requirements, character limits with regex validation on free-form fields, and manual takedown under the moderation policy
A $100 listing fee
A CAPTCHA per API call
Nothing; spam is allowed

questions.explanation: Publishers must prove namespace ownership (GitHub, DNS, or HTTP challenges), fields are limited and validated, and maintainers can remove spam or malicious servers per the moderation policy. Rate limiting and AI-based detection are under consideration.

questions.question: SCENARIO: After publishing, you want to confirm your server io.github.my-username/weather is live. What's the documented way?

options.text: Wait for a confirmation email
Query the registry API, e.g., curl "https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io/v0.1/servers?search=io.github.my-username/weather", and check your server's metadata appears in the results JSON
Run npm view on the registry
Check the GitHub Actions tab of the registry repo

questions.explanation: The quickstart's verification step is a search against the public REST API; your server.json metadata (name, version, packages, remotes) should come back in the servers array.

questions.question: How do other registries interoperate with the official MCP Registry?

options.text: They must mirror its database verbatim
The registry defines an OpenAPI spec that downstream aggregators and private registries can implement, giving host applications a standardized interface regardless of which registry they consume
Interoperability is prohibited
Via nightly FTP dumps

questions.explanation: Beyond the hosted service, the project publishes an OpenAPI specification. Aggregators and private registries implementing it benefit from existing host application support — though the official codebase itself is not designed for self-hosting.

questions.question: What does an MCP version identifier like 2026-07-28 actually denote?

options.text: The date the documentation website was updated
A YYYY-MM-DD version label marking the last date backwards-incompatible changes were made to the specification
The server's build date
A semantic version in disguise

questions.explanation: MCP uses date-stamped string version identifiers (YYYY-MM-DD) indicating the last date of backwards-incompatible changes. 2026-07-28 replaced 2025-11-25.

questions.question: What is the single headline change of the 2026-07-28 revision?

options.text: A switch from JSON to Protocol Buffers
MCP became stateless at the protocol layer: no initialize handshake, no protocol-level sessions, so servers run behind ordinary load balancers and on serverless platforms
Mandatory paid licensing
Removal of the tools primitive

questions.explanation: Six SEPs together made MCP a request/response stateless protocol — the most requested change for reliability and scalability of remote servers.

questions.question: Which handshake did 2026-07-28 remove, and what replaced it?

options.text: The TLS handshake, replaced by QUIC
The initialize/notifications/initialized handshake, replaced by per-request _meta fields (protocolVersion, clientCapabilities, clientInfo) plus the mandatory server/discover RPC
OAuth consent, replaced by API keys
tools/list, replaced by server/discover

questions.explanation: SEP-2575: the handshake is gone; every request self-describes via _meta, servers should identify themselves via serverInfo in each result's _meta, and server/discover (which servers MUST implement) provides up-front version/capability discovery.

questions.question: What is the required resultType field introduced in 2026-07-28?

options.text: A MIME type for the payload

A discriminator on every result: "complete" for ordinary results, "input_required" for MRTR interim results (and "task" reserved for the Tasks extension); results from earlier-protocol servers that omit it are treated as "complete"
A boolean success flag
The name of the SDK that produced the result

questions.explanation: SEP-2322 made resultType required so clients can parse results polymorphically: complete vs input_required (MRTR), with 'task' reserved by the Tasks extension. Missing field from legacy servers → treat as complete.

questions.question: Which methods were removed outright in 2026-07-28?

options.text: tools/list and prompts/get
ping, logging/setLevel, and notifications/roots/list_changed (log level moved to per-request _meta; resources/subscribe & unsubscribe and the HTTP GET endpoint were replaced by subscriptions/listen)
elicitation/create
server/discover

questions.explanation: The changelog lists ping, logging/setLevel, and notifications/roots/list_changed as removed; logging is now per-request via io.modelcontextprotocol/logLevel, and change notifications consolidated onto subscriptions/listen.

questions.question: Under the feature lifecycle policy adopted in 2026-07-28, what states can a specification feature be in, and what's the minimum deprecation window?

options.text: Alpha, Beta, GA — 30 days
Active, Deprecated, Removed — with a minimum twelve-month deprecation window and a registry of deprecated features
Draft, Final — no window
Experimental, Stable, Legacy — 6 months

questions.explanation: SEP-2596 defines Active/Deprecated/Removed, a minimum 12-month window (deprecated features keep working in this version and every version published within a year), and a deprecated-features registry. Actual removal needs a separate explicit proposal.

questions.question: SCENARIO: Your production server heavily uses Sampling. It's deprecated in 2026-07-28. Do you need an emergency migration before July 28?

options.text: Yes; deprecated features stop working on release day

No — deprecated features remain fully functional for at least the twelve-month window; nothing breaks on release day, but new implementations shouldn't adopt them and you should plan migration to direct LLM provider APIs
Only if you also use Roots
Sampling was removed, not deprecated

questions.explanation: Per the maintainers, 'nothing breaks on July 28': Roots, Sampling, and Logging (SEP-2577) keep working for at least twelve months. Migration paths: tool params/config for roots, direct LLM APIs for sampling, stderr/OpenTelemetry for logging.

questions.question: What changed about client registration in the 2026-07-28 authorization stack?

options.text: Registration is no longer required

Dynamic Client Registration (RFC 7591) was deprecated in favor of Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD); DCR remains available for backwards compatibility with authorization servers that don't support CIMD
Only static pre-registration is allowed now
CIMD was deprecated in favor of DCR

questions.explanation: The changelog deprecates DCR as the registration mechanism: CIMD (URL-based client IDs proving domain control) is the way forward, with DCR kept for compatibility until a future removal.

questions.question: Which OAuth hardening did 2026-07-28 add regarding the iss parameter?

options.text: iss was removed from responses

Authorization servers SHOULD include iss in authorization responses (RFC 9207), and clients MUST validate a present iss against the recorded issuer before redeeming the authorization code — mitigating mix-up attacks
iss now carries the access token
Clients must ignore iss

questions.explanation: SEP-2468: issuer identification in authorization responses binds the response to the expected authorization server, preventing mix-up attacks where a code would be redeemed at an attacker's token endpoint.

questions.question: How did 2026-07-28 repartition the JSON-RPC server-error code range for MCP?

options.text: MCP now uses positive error codes

-32000 to -32019 stays implementation-defined (existing SDK usage grandfathered) and -32020 to -32099 is reserved for the MCP spec; draft codes were renumbered (HeaderMismatch → -32020, MissingRequiredClientCapability → -32021, UnsupportedProtocolVersion → -32022)
All errors collapsed into -32603
Error codes are now strings

questions.explanation: The error code allocation policy splits the JSON-RPC server-error range and renumbered the new errors accordingly; resource-not-found also moved from -32002 to -32602 to align with JSON-RPC Invalid Params.

questions.question: In the versioning docs and Inspector terminology, what defines the 'legacy' vs 'modern' protocol eras?

options.text: Legacy = stdio; modern = HTTP
Legacy uses the initialize handshake (2025-11-25 and earlier); modern uses per-request protocol metadata (2026-07-28 and later); dual-era implementations deliberately support both
Legacy = open source; modern = commercial
The eras differ only in default port numbers

questions.explanation: The era split: a modern-only client can't talk to a legacy-only server and vice versa — version negotiation detects the mismatch but doesn't bridge it. Dual-era servers answer the legacy initialize alongside server/discover, which is how nothing broke on release day.

questions.question: SCENARIO: Your remote MCP server must serve both a 2025-11-25 IDE plugin and a 2026-07-28 agent. What's the recommended approach?

options.text: Run two separate domains forever
Serve dual-era: answer the legacy initialize handshake alongside server/discover; SDKs route per request (e.g., by the MCP-Protocol-Version header or its absence) so one deployment handles both eras
Reject legacy clients with 426 Upgrade Required
Downgrade the server to legacy-only

questions.explanation: New-spec servers can be dual-era: SDKs route requests by the protocol version they name (legacy clients' initialize carries no modern header), so 2025-11-25 clients keep connecting while 2026-07-28 clients get the stateless path.

questions.question: What happened to the old HTTP+SSE transport in 2026-07-28?

options.text: It became the default transport
Already superseded since 2025-03-26, it was formally reclassified as Deprecated under the lifecycle policy with a year-long offramp; migrate to Streamable HTTP
It was renamed Streamable HTTP
It was extended with HTTP/3 support

questions.explanation: SEP-2596 reclassified the legacy HTTP+SSE transport as Deprecated. The includeContext values 'thisServer'/'allServers' were also reclassified as Deprecated in the same sweep.

questions.question: What observability convention did 2026-07-28 document for _meta?

options.text: A new binary tracing format
OpenTelemetry / W3C Trace Context propagation via the traceparent, tracestate, and baggage keys (SEP-414), so distributed traces correlate across host, SDK, server, and downstream calls
Mandatory Prometheus metrics
Logging every payload to stdout

questions.explanation: Locking down these _meta key names means a trace starting in a host application can follow a tool call through the client SDK, the MCP server, and downstream systems as a single span tree.

questions.question: SCENARIO: Under the SDK tiering system, what were Tier 1 SDKs expected to do during the ten-week release-candidate window (locked May 21, final July 28, 2026)?

options.text: Nothing; SDKs update whenever convenient
Ship support for the new specification within the validation window, so implementers could validate the changes against real workloads before the final release
Freeze all releases entirely
Rewrite themselves in Rust

questions.explanation: The RC window existed for SDK maintainers and client implementers to validate against real workloads; under the SDK tier system Tier 1 SDKs (TypeScript, Python, and peers) were expected to ship support within it — and all four spoke 2026-07-28 on release day.

questions.question: Under what legal structure and licenses does the MCP project operate?

options.text: A private Anthropic subsidiary; all rights reserved
Model Context Protocol, a Series of LF Projects, LLC; code and specification contributions under Apache 2.0, documentation (excluding specs) under CC BY 4.0
A Delaware C-corp; MIT license
An informal GitHub org with no legal entity

questions.explanation: MCP is established as 'Model Context Protocol a Series of LF Projects, LLC'. Code/spec contributions use Apache License 2.0; documentation is CC BY 4.0. Contributors retain copyright — no assignment to the project is required.

questions.question: What is the technical governance hierarchy of the MCP project?

options.text: A flat structure where all contributors vote equally
Contributors → Maintainers → Core Maintainers → Lead Maintainers (BDFL), modeled on projects like Python and PyTorch
A board of corporate seat-holders
Anthropic employees only

questions.explanation: The hierarchy runs Contributors (issues/PRs) → Maintainers (SDKs, docs, Working Groups) → Core Maintainers (project direction) → Lead Maintainers (final decision authority, a.k.a. BDFL). Together the maintainer tiers form the MCP Steering Group.

questions.question: What is a defining rule of maintainer membership in MCP governance?

options.text: Seats are reserved for founding companies
Membership is tied to individuals, not companies — no reserved corporate seats, merit-based, no term limit, and it stays with the person if they change employers
Membership rotates alphabetically each quarter
Only Anthropic staff may be Core Maintainers

questions.explanation: Governance membership is explicitly individual: no company seats, granted on merit after demonstrated expertise, associated with the person rather than the employer, and without term limits. This prioritizes protocol integrity over corporate interests.

questions.question: What can Lead Maintainers do that Core Maintainers cannot?

options.text: Merge pull requests
Veto any decision by Core Maintainers or Maintainers (BDFL authority), and appoint or remove Core Maintainers — while being expected to publicly articulate their reasoning
Write to SDK repositories
Participate in Working Groups

questions.explanation: Lead Maintainers hold final authority: veto over any decision and the power to appoint/remove Core Maintainers, plus admin on all project infrastructure. Core Maintainers can veto Maintainer decisions by majority vote and appoint/remove Maintainers, but not override the Leads.

questions.question: SCENARIO: A Core Maintainer wants to change the specification repo. Per governance rules, how must they proceed?

options.text: Push directly to main — they have admin access
Use the same pull-request contribution process as external contributors, providing visibility into intent and opportunity for discussion
Email the change to the other maintainers
Open a private Discord vote first, then push directly

questions.explanation: Maintainers at every level (Maintainers, Core, Lead) should use the same contribution process as external contributors rather than making direct changes — despite having write/admin access.

questions.question: What is the difference between Interest Groups and Working Groups in MCP?

options.text: They are two names for the same thing
Interest Groups identify and articulate problems MCP should address through open discussion; Working Groups develop concrete solutions, producing deliverables like SEPs or implementations
Interest Groups write code; Working Groups write blog posts
Working Groups are for companies, Interest Groups for individuals

questions.explanation: The two collaboration structures split problem-space from solution-space: IGs surface and articulate problems; WGs (formalized under SEP-1302) produce SEPs and implementations that solve them.

questions.question: How does the Core Maintainer group make and communicate decisions?

options.text: Annual closed-door summits with sealed minutes

Bi-weekly meetings to discuss and vote on proposals, with notes made public; a shared Discord server for maintainer coordination where decisions and supporting discussions must be recorded transparently; in-person meetings targeted every 3–6 months
Decisions are made solely by GitHub reactions
There is no defined decision process

questions.explanation: The cadence is bi-weekly Core Maintainer meetings (public proposal notes), Discord as the recorded governance channel, and in-person meetings every three to six months.

questions.question: Which roles does the Contributor Ladder define OUTSIDE the MCP Steering Group?

options.text: Member and Community Moderator
Intern and Apprentice
Sponsor and Auditor
There are no roles outside the Steering Group

questions.explanation: The Contributor Ladder is the canonical definition of all roles — requirements, privileges, advancement, inactivity policy — and includes Member and Community Moderator, which sit outside the Steering Group (Maintainers + Core + Lead).

questions.question: How should a security vulnerability in an MCP SDK be reported?

options.text: Open a public GitHub issue with full reproduction details
Through GitHub Security Advisories (private vulnerability reporting) on the affected repository — never via public issues, discussions, or pull requests
Post it on the public Discord
Email it to any maintainer's personal address

questions.explanation: Private vulnerability reporting is enabled on the specification repo and every official SDK repo in the modelcontextprotocol org. Public channels are explicitly ruled out for security reports.

questions.question: How are CVEs assigned for MCP vulnerabilities?

options.text: Through GitHub's CNA as part of the GHSA (GitHub Security Advisory) workflow
Anthropic operates its own CNA
MCP does not use CVEs
Reporters must request CVEs directly from MITRE

questions.explanation: CVE assignment rides the GHSA workflow via GitHub's CVE Numbering Authority — no separate process is needed once the private advisory is filed.

questions.question: SCENARIO: A vulnerability report is filed against the Python SDK, and the flaw stems from a transport pattern all official SDKs implement the same way. What does the security policy say happens next?

options.text: Each SDK team handles it independently whenever they notice

The receiving maintainers assess cross-SDK impact and coordinate with other SDK maintainers so fixes and advisories release together — and if the root cause is a spec defect, they escalate to the specification maintainers
The report is closed as out of scope
The reporter must re-file against every SDK repo

questions.explanation: Many MCP vulnerabilities stem from shared patterns or spec-level behavior. The policy mandates cross-SDK coordination for simultaneous release (so no SDK is left exposed after others publish) and escalation to spec maintainers when the specification itself is the defect.

questions.question: Why are 'stdio peer attacks' generally OUT of scope as vulnerabilities?

options.text: Because stdio is deprecated

Because the client spawns the server locally and both may run at equivalent privilege: a malicious server already has arbitrary code execution by being run, and a malicious client has full process control over the server — the stdio transport is not a sandbox
Because stdio traffic is encrypted
Because the OS prevents such attacks

questions.explanation: The trust model treats stdio peers as within one trust boundary. Reports whose only impact is one stdio peer crashing, hanging, or DoS-ing the other are regular issues, not GHSAs. They come back IN scope if the code is reachable via remote transports or causes a sandbox escape.

questions.question: SCENARIO: A researcher finds that a malicious stdio server can hang its client with malformed output — and the same parsing code also runs in the Streamable HTTP transport. In scope or not?

options.text: Out of scope — anything involving stdio peers is excluded
In scope — the stdio-peer exclusion falls away when the affected SDK code is reachable via a supported remote transport (or results in a sandbox escape)
In scope only if a CVE already exists
Out of scope because DoS never qualifies

questions.explanation: The exclusion is narrow: stdio-peer-only impact is out of scope, but reachability through remote transports (where the attacker is NOT a co-privileged local process) brings the same defect back into scope for a private advisory.

questions.question: Which issue classes does the security policy list as in-scope vulnerabilities when caused by flaws in the spec or official SDKs?

options.text: Protocol-level vulnerabilities, authentication/authorization bypasses, injection and memory-safety bugs, sandbox escapes, session hijacking, token leakage, and cross-tenant access
Only remote code execution
Typos in documentation
Performance regressions

questions.explanation: That is the policy's scope list verbatim in substance — spanning protocol design flaws through implementation bugs to isolation failures.

questions.question: What does the Security Interest Group do — and which security topics does it explicitly NOT own?

options.text: It owns every security topic in the project

It discusses MCP-specific threats, reviews security-relevant proposals, and routes disclosure questions; but OAuth flow mechanics belong to the Authorization IG, TLS/mTLS to the Transports WG, tool-annotation design to the Tool Annotations IG, and registry service operation to the Registry WG
It only writes CVE descriptions
It audits third-party servers for a fee

questions.explanation: The SIG charter is deliberately scoped: cross-cutting threat discussion, proposal review, and disclosure routing (a known contact for reporters who can't reach the right maintainer) — with adjacent domains delegated to their own groups.

questions.question: What is the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF)?

options.text: A commercial marketplace for AI agents
A vendor-neutral foundation under the Linux Foundation, announced December 9, 2025, that serves as the open-governance home for the agentic AI stack
Anthropic's internal research division
A certification body that licenses AI models

questions.explanation: The Linux Foundation announced the AAIF on December 9, 2025 as a neutral home where the open standard agentic AI stack is built — governing core standards and protocols so agents can interoperate across platforms, with no single company dominating.

questions.question: Which projects anchored the AAIF at its founding?

options.text: Kubernetes, Docker, and Terraform
MCP (contributed by Anthropic), goose (Block), AGENTS.md (OpenAI), and agentgateway
TensorFlow and PyTorch
Only MCP

questions.explanation: The founding project contributions were Anthropic's Model Context Protocol, Block's goose, and OpenAI's AGENTS.md, with agentgateway also among the founding projects — uniting competing vendors' key agentic projects under one neutral roof.

questions.question: What is goose?

options.text: A benchmark suite for LLMs
Block's open-source, local-first AI agent framework that combines language models, extensible tools, and standardized MCP-based integration
An MCP server for bird-watching data
OpenAI's coding assistant

questions.explanation: goose is Block's contribution: an open-source, local-first agent framework whose tool integration is standardized on MCP — also a canonical example of an MCP host application.

questions.question: What is AGENTS.md?

options.text: The changelog file of the MCP repository
A simple, universal standard (contributed by OpenAI) giving AI coding agents a consistent source of project-specific guidance so they operate reliably across repositories and toolchains
A registry of approved AI agents
MCP's authorization configuration file

questions.explanation: AGENTS.md (initially released August 2025, contributed by OpenAI to the AAIF) standardizes how repos hand project-specific instructions to coding agents; it's been adopted by tens of thousands of open-source projects and integrated by tools like Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and VS Code.

questions.question: What is agentgateway?

options.text: An MCP gateway/proxy project in the AAIF for mediating agent and MCP traffic
A paid API rate limiter from Anthropic
The Registry's REST endpoint
A browser extension for MCP Apps

questions.explanation: agentgateway (originally from Solo.io) is the AAIF's gateway/proxy project — infrastructure that sits in front of agent/MCP traffic, exactly the layer that benefits from 2026-07-28's Mcp-Method/Mcp-Name header routing.

questions.question: Why did Anthropic donate MCP to a foundation rather than keep sole control?

options.text: Regulatory requirements forced the transfer

Neutral, open governance ensures the protocol evolves by community consensus rather than one company's roadmap — protecting downstream developers from unilateral changes and encouraging competitors to adopt a standard no rival controls
To sell the trademark
Because MCP was feature-complete and needed no further development

questions.explanation: The AAIF rationale: when connection protocols are owned by a single vendor, every downstream developer is exposed to unilateral pricing/compatibility/deprecation decisions. Neutral stewardship under the Linux Foundation model is what lets AWS, Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI all invest in the same standard.

questions.question: Which companies were platinum members of the AAIF at launch?

options.text: Only Anthropic and Block
Amazon Web Services, Anthropic, Block, Bloomberg, Cloudflare, Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI
Apple, Meta, and Netflix
The foundation has no corporate members

questions.explanation: The launch platinum tier spanned the competitive landscape: AWS, Anthropic, Block, Bloomberg, Cloudflare, Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI — rivals cooperating on shared agentic infrastructure.

questions.question: SCENARIO: On the exam, you're asked which ecosystem role each party plays: a database company shipping an MCP server, a startup building an AI assistant, and Claude Desktop / goose. Match them.

options.text: Tool provider → builds MCP servers; app developer → builds MCP clients; Claude Desktop and goose → host applications
All three are hosts
The database company builds clients; the startup builds servers
Hosts are only built by Anthropic

questions.explanation: The who-builds-what triad: tool/data providers expose servers, application developers implement clients inside their products, and hosts (Claude Desktop, goose, IDEs) coordinate clients and the LLM.

questions.question: What is the core portability benefit MCP gives the ecosystem?

options.text: Servers run faster on ARM processors
Write a server once and it works in any compliant MCP client/host — no vendor lock-in, and each new server or client enriches the whole ecosystem
Free hosting for all servers
Automatic translation of tools into every programming language

questions.explanation: Because the protocol is the contract, a weather server built for Claude Desktop also works in goose, Cursor, or VS Code — the M+N economics compound as the ecosystem grows.

questions.question: SCENARIO: An exam question claims 'MCP is governed by Anthropic, which holds final authority over the specification.' What's wrong with that statement in 2026?

options.text: Nothing — Anthropic owns MCP

MCP was contributed to the AAIF under the Linux Foundation; it's governed by the community model (SEPs, Working Groups, individual-based maintainer hierarchy) — Anthropic created MCP but no company holds governance seats or final authority
Google holds final authority
The Linux Foundation writes all SEPs itself

questions.explanation: Post-donation, governance is vendor-neutral: maintainer membership is individual (explicitly not corporate), Lead Maintainers hold BDFL authority within the community model, and the AAIF/LF provides the legal umbrella. 'Created by Anthropic' remains true; 'governed by Anthropic' does not.
